qs.q: <svg width="320" height="140" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#fff;"><rect x="10" y="10" width="90" height="40" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/><text x="55" y="34" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif">Executive</text><rect x="115" y="10" width="90" height="40" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/><text x="160" y="34" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif">Legislature</text><rect x="220" y="10" width="90" height="40" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/><text x="265" y="34" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif">Judiciary</text><path d="M 100 20 L 115 20 M 115 40 L 100 40 M 205 20 L 220 20 M 220 40 L 205 40" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="10" y="80" width="300" height="45" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="160" y="107" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif">Constitutional System of Checks & Balances</text></svg> Examining the tripartite institutional relationship in the diagram, if the President rejects a passed law, which specific action by the Legislature overrules that veto?
o: Filing an appeal before the International Court of Justice
Issuing an executive decree signed by the Senate President
Dissolving the Cabinet and calling immediate snap elections
Two-thirds majority vote override in both legislative chambers
qs.e: In presidential constitutional systems, if the President exercises a veto, the legislature can override the presidential veto by repassing the bill with a two-thirds supermajority vote in both chambers.

qs.q: A legislative bill introduced by an individual member of parliament who is not a cabinet minister or executive official is formally classified as a
qs.e: A Private Member's Bill is proposed by a legislator in their personal capacity, whereas an Executive Bill is introduced on behalf of the government executive.

qs.q: In a cabinet system of government, if the legislature passes a vote of no confidence against the Prime Minister, what is the mandatory constitutional outcome?
o: Only the Speaker of the House is dismissed from office
The Prime Minister and the entire Cabinet must resign
The Chief Justice assumes full executive government control
The bill is referred to state governors for ratification
qs.e: Under collective cabinet responsibility in a parliamentary system, a vote of no confidence against the Prime Minister forces the resignation of the entire executive cabinet.

qs.q: Under Section 232 of the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, the Supreme Court exercises original jurisdiction exclusively in legal disputes between
o: Individual citizens claiming breach of contract
Local government councils and traditional rulers
The Federation and a State, or between States
Registered political parties and electoral officers
qs.e: Section 232 grants the Supreme Court original jurisdiction (acting as the trial court) in disputes between the Federal Government and States, or between States themselves.

qs.q: When a federal law and a state law conflict on a subject listed on the Concurrent Legislative List, the constitutional principle dictating that the federal law prevails is the
qs.e: Under the Doctrine of Covering the Field, where federal legislation validly covers a subject on the concurrent list, any state law inconsistent with it becomes void to the extent of the inconsistency.

qs.q: Unlike the 1951 Macpherson Constitution, the 1954 Lyttelton Constitution established true federalism in Nigeria by
o: Creating autonomous regional civil services and judiciaries
Abolishing regional Houses of Assembly in the North
Adopting a unitary system under a Governor-General
Granting universal adult suffrage exclusively in the North
qs.e: The 1954 Lyttelton Constitution established formal federalism by granting autonomous powers, separate civil services, and regional judiciaries to the Northern, Western, and Eastern regions.

qs.q: Following the December 1959 pre-independence federal elections, no single political party won an absolute majority of seats in the House of Representatives. Consequently, federal government was formed through a coalition between the
o: Action Group (AG) and Northern Elements Progressive Union (NEPU)
Northern People's Congress (NPC) and United Middle Belt Congress (UMBC)
qs.e: The 1959 election resulted in a hung parliament. The NPC (led by Ahmadu Bello/Balewa) formed a coalition government with Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe's NCNC, making Balewa Prime Minister and Azikiwe Senate President.

qs.q: A professional association submits policy research papers and testifies before a parliamentary committee on proposed tax regulations. This method of pressure group operation is known as
qs.e: Lobbying involves contacting, persuading, and supplying expert information to legislators and policymakers to influence legislative outcomes without seeking public office.

qs.q: In an electoral system utilizing the Absolute Majority rule, if four candidates contest an election and the top candidate receives 42% of votes, what procedure must follow?
o: Immediate declaration of the top candidate as winner
Cancellation of the election and appointment of a administrator
Allocation of legislative seats by proportional percentage
A runoff election between the top two candidates
qs.e: Under absolute majority rules, a winning candidate must achieve over 50% of valid votes. If no candidate reaches this threshold in the first round, a second round (runoff) is required.

qs.q: Which cadre of the civil service is primarily tasked with high-level policy advice, administrative planning, and drafting executive memoranda for ministers?
qs.e: The Administrative Cadre comprises top-tier civil servants (e.g. Permanent Secretaries, Directors) who advise ministers and formulate policy guidelines.

qs.q: The landmark 1976 Local Government Reforms in Nigeria achieved structural uniformity nationwide by
o: Subordinating local councils directly to traditional rulers
Establishing single-tier local government councils across all states
Abolishing direct statutory revenue allocations from the center
Merging local government administration with state judiciaries
qs.e: The 1976 reforms introduced a uniform, single-tier local government system across all states in Nigeria, recognizing local government as the formal third tier of governance.

qs.q: A foreign national who has resided in Nigeria for over fifteen years applies for Nigerian citizenship. Which method of acquisition is being pursued?
qs.e: Citizenship by naturalization is granted to foreign nationals who satisfy constitutional residency requirements (at least 15 years), demonstrate good character, and renounce previous nationality.

qs.q: During the Cold War, Nigeria's foreign policy adhered to Non-Alignment. In practice, this meant Nigeria
o: Severed diplomatic relations with all permanent members of the UN Security Council
Formed an exclusive military pact with neighbouring West African states only
Accepted military directives strictly from the Commonwealth Prime Ministers
Refused formal military alignment with either the Western or Eastern power blocs
qs.e: Non-alignment meant refusing to join military alliances with either the US-led Western bloc or Soviet-led Eastern bloc, maintaining independent decision-making in global affairs.

qs.q: Which UN organ bears primary constitutional responsibility for maintaining international peace and security and possesses the authority to authorize military action?
qs.e: Under the UN Charter, the Security Council holds primary responsibility for international peace and security and can adopt binding resolutions and authorize military enforcement.

qs.q: General Aguiyi-Ironsi promulgated Decree No. 34 of 1966 (the Unification Decree). The major political consequence of this decree was the
o: Abolition of the federal structure and creation of a unitary administrative system
Establishment of twelve new states across the federation
Creation of the Independent National Electoral Commission
qs.e: Decree No. 34 abolished Nigeria's federal structure, centralized civil services, and instituted a unitary system, triggering severe political friction and the July 1966 counter-coup.

qs.q: A state governor issues an executive order banning all public political gatherings. A civil rights organization challenges this order in court as violating freedom of assembly. The court strikes down the order. This judicial decision illustrates
o: Judicial review protecting constitutional fundamental rights
qs.e: Judicial review enables courts to invalidate executive or legislative actions that infringe upon constitutionally guaranteed fundamental human rights.

qs.q: Which ideological political model advocates the complete elimination of state authority, police forces, and statutory laws in favor of voluntary self-governing associations?
qs.e: Anarchism opposes all forms of compulsory government authority and state machinery, advocating voluntary stateless cooperation.

qs.q: A key structural weakness of an unwritten constitution in a developing democracy is that it
o: Lacks a single codified document, making rights protection reliant on precedent and convention
Cannot be altered by ordinary legislative statutory amendments
Prevents parliament from enacting statutory economic laws
Mandates a rigid federal division of powers between regions
qs.e: Unwritten constitutions rely on judicial precedents, statutes, and historical conventions rather than a single codified supreme text, which can create ambiguity in rights protection.

qs.q: In political science, political socialization refers to the process through which
o: Political parties merge during general election campaigns
Individuals acquire political values, beliefs, and attitudes from childhood through adulthood
Government agencies nationalize private commercial firms
State governors draft statutory local government budgets
qs.e: Political socialization is the lifelong process by which citizens learn political culture, orientations, and civic values through agents like family, schools, and media.

qs.q: When a minister appears before a legislative committee to answer questions regarding expenditure in their ministry, this legislative action is an exercise of
qs.e: Legislative oversight is the monitoring and evaluation of executive implementation of laws and budgetary funds by parliamentary committees.

qs.q: In a presidential system of government, cabinet ministers are accountable primarily to the
o: Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
qs.e: In a presidential system, ministers serve as advisers accountable directly to the President (individual responsibility), unlike the collective cabinet responsibility in parliamentary systems.

qs.q: The doctrine of locus standi requires a plaintiff filing a constitutional challenge in court to prove that they
o: Sustained direct legal injury or personal interest in the matter
Possess unanimous backing from a registered political party
Hold an elective political office in the state legislature
Obtained prior written clearance from the Attorney General
qs.e: Locus standi (standing to sue) requires a litigant to establish a sufficient legal interest or direct injury in a case before a court will adjudicate the suit.

qs.q: Which revenue allocation principle asserts that states generating natural resources should receive a higher percentage of revenues derived from those resources?
qs.e: The derivation principle allocates a specific percentage of national revenue directly back to the state or region where the natural resource was extracted.

qs.q: The 1963 Republican Constitution of Nigeria fundamentally altered the 1960 Independence structure by replacing the British Queen as Head of State with a ceremonial President who was
qs.e: Under the 1963 Republican Constitution, Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe became Nigeria's first ceremonial Head of State, cutting constitutional ties with the British Monarchy.

qs.q: In the 1979 Second Republic elections, the political party led by Chief Obafemi Awolowo that implemented the 'Four Cardinal Programmes' (including free education) was the
qs.e: The UPN, led by Obafemi Awolowo in the Second Republic, campaigned on four cardinal programmes: free education, free healthcare, rural development, and full employment.

qs.q: Anomic pressure groups are distinguished from associational pressure groups because anomic groups
o: Form spontaneously in response to a sudden crisis without permanent organizational structure
Possess permanent headquarters and professional secretariats
Operate strictly through commercial legal practitioners in court
Limit membership exclusively to active military officers
qs.e: Anomic pressure groups are short-lived, spontaneous crowds or riot groups that emerge unexpectedly in response to specific emotional triggers or crises.

qs.q: In proportional representation systems, legislative seats are awarded to political parties based on
o: Which candidate wins the highest votes in individual single-member constituencies
The overall percentage of votes the party receives nationally or in multi-member districts
The length of time the political party has been officially registered
Direct appointments made by the electoral commission chairman
qs.e: Proportional representation allocates parliamentary seats proportionally according to the percentage of total votes each party secures.

qs.q: The 1988 Dotun Philips Civil Service Reform in Nigeria attempted to professionalize the civil service by changing the designation of Permanent Secretary to
qs.e: The 1988 reform redesignated Permanent Secretaries as Directors-General and made the position political, terminating tenure upon the exit of the appointing minister.

qs.q: A public corporation differs structurally from a civil service ministry because a public corporation
o: Is headed directly by an elected member of parliament
Derives all its operational funds exclusively from local government rates
Is staffed entirely by military officers on secondment
Possesses independent legal personality and can sue or be sued in its own name
qs.e: Public corporations are statutory bodies endowed with corporate legal personality, enabling them to hold property, enter contracts, and sue or be sued independently.

qs.q: According to the Fourth Schedule of the 1999 Constitution, which of the following is a primary function of local government councils in Nigeria?
o: Establishment and maintenance of public markets, motor parks, and street naming
Printing and issuing of national currency notes
Commanding military defense formations along state borders
qs.e: The 4th Schedule lists local government functions, including markets, motor parks, street naming, sewage disposal, and registration of births/deaths.

qs.q: Under Nigerian nationality law, dual citizenship is permissible under which specific constitutional condition?
o: For foreign naturalized citizens who retain their original passports
For citizens by birth who acquire citizenship of another country
For diplomatic officers serving in foreign embassies only
For non-citizens appointed to federal civil service boards
qs.e: Under Section 28 of the 1999 Constitution, a Nigerian citizen by birth does not lose Nigerian citizenship upon acquiring the citizenship of another country.

qs.q: The establishment of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) in May 1975 was driven primarily by diplomatic initiatives led by Nigeria and
qs.e: ECOWAS was created through the joint diplomatic efforts of Nigeria (under General Yakubu Gowon) and Togo (under President Gnassingbe Eyadema) in signing the 1975 Treaty of Lagos.

qs.q: The Commonwealth of Nations is best described as a voluntary association of independent sovereign states that are predominantly
o: Oil-exporting nations located in the Global South
Permanent members of the UN Security Council
Francophone West African states sharing a common currency
Former territories and colonies of the former British Empire
qs.e: The Commonwealth is an association of sovereign states comprising mostly former colonies of the British Empire working together on democracy, development, and trade.

qs.q: General Yakubu Gowon created 12 states in May 1967 primarily to
o: Weaken Eastern regional secessionist moves and satisfy minority ethnic demands
Abolish local government councils in Northern Nigeria
Hand over government power immediately to civilian politicians
Implement the 1976 Local Government Reforms early
qs.e: Gowon broke the 4 regional structures into 12 states in May 1967 to preempt Eastern regional secession (Biafra) and address long-standing minority grievances.

qs.q: In political science, political culture is classified into parochial, subject, and participant cultures. In a participant political culture, citizens
o: Have zero awareness of central political institutions and live in isolated tribal units
Are highly conscious of political institutions and actively participate in civic and political life
Are aware of government authority but remain passive subjects without participating in decision-making
Reject all constitutional governance in favor of military autocracy
qs.e: In Almond and Verba's typology, a participant political culture features citizens who actively engage in political processes, vote, and hold leaders accountable.

qs.q: The economic doctrine that advocates state collective ownership of land and communal labor based on traditional African socio-political structures is known as
qs.e: Communalism is the traditional African socio-economic organization centered on shared land ownership, mutual community assistance, and collective welfare.

qs.q: Which constitutional feature guarantees that no single branch of government can act ultra vires without exposure to judicial or legislative restraint?
qs.e: Checks and balances give each arm of government mechanisms to limit and review the actions of the other two arms, upholding constitutional limits.

qs.q: The writ of Habeas Corpus is a vital judicial instrument under the Rule of Law used to
o: Compel law enforcement to bring a detained individual before a court to determine the legality of detention
Prevent parliament from debating controversial tax legislation
Grant executive pardon to convicted political prisoners
Dissolve local government councils failing to collect tenancy rates
qs.e: Habeas corpus is a court order commanding the custodian of a prisoner to produce the person in court and show lawful cause for their detention.

qs.q: A legislative motion used to limit debate on a bill and force an immediate vote is known as the
qs.e: Cloture (or closure) is a parliamentary procedure used to end debate and bring a question/bill to an immediate vote.

qs.q: Delegated legislation issued by statutory public bodies or local councils in the form of administrative rules or orders is called
qs.e: Delegated (secondary) legislation includes statutory instruments and local council bye-laws enacted under authority delegated by the legislature.

qs.q: The appointment of judicial officers to the Supreme Court of Nigeria requires nomination by the National Judicial Council (NJC), confirmation by the Senate, and formal appointment by the
o: President of the Court of Appeal
qs.e: Under Section 231 of the 1999 Constitution, Supreme Court justices are appointed by the President on the recommendation of the NJC, subject to Senate confirmation.

qs.q: The Residual Legislative List under Nigeria's federal constitution comprises all legislative subjects
o: Not listed on either the Exclusive or Concurrent Lists, reserved exclusively for State Houses of Assembly
Shared concurrently between the Federal Parliament and Local Government Councils
Vested exclusively in the Federal Executive Council for emergency decrees
Managed jointly by the Supreme Court and Federal Character Commission
qs.e: Residual matters are subjects omitted from both Exclusive and Concurrent lists; under federal principles, residual legislative power belongs to the states.

qs.q: The Willink Commission established in 1957 by the British colonial government was specifically tasked with
o: Drafting the economic framework for nationalizing public corporations
Inquiring into the fears of minority ethnic groups and recommending means of allaying them
Recommending the abolition of traditional chieftaincy institutions
qs.e: The 1957 Willink Commission investigated minority fears in the North, West, and East prior to independence, recommending a fundamental rights bill rather than new regions.

qs.q: The political party formed in 1951 by Chief Obafemi Awolowo which evolved from the Yoruba cultural organization Egbe Omo Oduduwa was the
o: National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC)
qs.e: The Action Group (AG) was founded in 1951 by Awolowo, developing out of Egbe Omo Oduduwa, and dominated the Western Region.

qs.q: Institutional pressure groups are distinguished by the fact that they operate within
o: Religious organizations focusing strictly on moral instruction
Multi-national corporate cartels operating outside statutory law
Formal governmental or state machinery such as the civil service or military officer corps
qs.e: Institutional pressure groups exist inside formal governmental or professional institutions (e.g. military cadres, senior civil servants) to advance structural interests.

qs.q: Gerrymandering refers to the controversial electoral practice of
o: Redrawing constituency boundaries deliberately to give an unfair advantage to a particular political party
Bribing electoral officials at polling centers to alter ballot tallies
Preventing citizens under 21 years of age from registering to vote
Cancelling general election results using executive military decrees
qs.e: Gerrymandering is the manipulation of electoral district boundaries to favour one political party or demographic group over others.

qs.q: Which major civil service reform panel in Nigeria restored the traditional career title of 'Permanent Secretary' and reaffirmed civil service security of tenure in 1997?
qs.e: The 1997 Allison Ayida Review Panel reversed major aspects of the 1988 Dotun Philips reform, restoring the title Permanent Secretary and career tenure.

qs.q: Red tape in public administration refers to
o: The formal ceremonial dress worn by judges in superior courts
Financial audit records maintained by the Auditor-General
Excessive adherence to rigid bureaucratic rules, formal procedures, and paperwork that causes delay
qs.e: Red tape denotes excessive bureaucracy, strict adherence to official rules, and elaborate paperwork that hinders administrative efficiency.

qs.q: Under local government administration in Nigeria, the State Joint Local Government Account is controlled jointly by state governments and local councils. Critics argue this mechanism often leads to
o: Total financial bankruptcy of the federal central government
Excessive financial independence of local councils from state control
Immediate conversion of local government staff into federal judges
State executive diversion and undue deduction of statutory local government funds
qs.e: The Joint Local Government Account has frequently been criticized because state governments exploit it to retain or divert statutory allocations meant for local councils.

qs.q: Deprivation of Nigerian citizenship acquired by naturalization can occur if the naturalized citizen is
o: Sentenced to imprisonment for a period of not less than three years within seven years of naturalization
Elected as a local government councillor in a rural district
Employed as a university lecturer in a federal institution
Granted an honorary chieftaincy title by a traditional ruler
qs.e: Under Section 26/27 of the 1999 Constitution, naturalized citizens can forfeit citizenship if convicted of severe offenses and sentenced to prison within 7 years.

qs.q: Nigeria contributed troops and spearheaded the formation of ECOMOG in 1990 under ECOWAS to restore peace in which West African country undergoing civil war?
qs.e: ECOMOG (ECOWAS Ceasefire Monitoring Group) was formed in 1990 under Nigerian leadership to intervene and stop the bloody civil war in Liberia.

qs.q: The Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) was established in 1960. Nigeria officially joined OPEC as a member nation in
qs.e: Nigeria joined OPEC in 1971 during General Yakubu Gowon's administration, securing influence over oil production quotas and pricing policies.

qs.q: General Murtala Muhammed's administration (1975–1976) gained immense popularity in Nigerian military history largely due to its
o: Promulgation of Decree No. 34 unifiying the civil service
Refusal to create new states in the federation
Indefinite postponement of return to democratic governance
Decisive, purge-driven anti-corruption campaign and clear transition plan to civilian rule
qs.e: Murtala Muhammed reinvigorated governance by launching a swift public service purge, creating 7 new states in 1976, and establishing a firm handover timeline.

qs.q: A dominant feature of a ONE-PARTY state governance structure is that
o: Only one official political party is constitutionally recognized and permitted to contest elections
Two parties alternate power through compulsory proportional representation
The judiciary exercises veto power over all party manifestos
Pressure groups are granted automatic legislative seats in parliament
qs.e: In a one-party state, opposition parties are banned or legally prohibited, leaving a single political party with exclusive political dominance.

qs.q: Which colonial constitution first established a single central Legislative Council that made laws for both the Northern and Southern Provinces of Nigeria together?
qs.e: The 1946 Richards Constitution brought Northern and Southern Nigeria under a single legislative framework for the first time in the central Legislative Council.

qs.q: In political governance, legitimacy is distinguished from legal power because legitimacy depends primarily on
o: The quantity of military weaponry controlled by the government
The size of the national legislative assembly
The broad acceptance and moral recognition of authority by the governed
The foreign economic aid received from international agencies
qs.e: Legitimacy is the moral right to rule based on the consent, trust, and acceptance of the citizens, distinguishing rightful authority from mere physical force.

qs.q: Lord Lugard's 1914 Amalgamation of Northern and Southern Nigeria was motivated primarily by administrative and financial considerations. Specifically, the British administration sought to
o: Establish a federal democratic structure with equal regional representation
Implement universal adult suffrage across both protectorates immediately
Create a unified judicial system based on Islamic Sharia law nationwide
Use the financial surplus of the Southern Protectorate to offset the administrative deficit of the North
qs.e: The primary economic driver for amalgamation in 1914 was to merge the financially self-supporting, revenue-surplus Southern Protectorate with the revenue-deficient Northern Protectorate to relieve the British Treasury of subsidies.

qs.q: Under the 1963 Republican Constitution of Nigeria, the ultimate judicial appellate authority was transferred from the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London to the
qs.e: The 1963 Republican Constitution cut final judicial ties with Britain by abolishing appeals to the Privy Council and making the Supreme Court of Nigeria the highest court of appeal.

qs.q: During the First Republic (1960–1966), the position of Prime Minister was held by Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, while Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe served first as Governor-General and later as ceremonial President. This arrangement exemplified
o: A dual executive structure within a parliamentary system
qs.e: The First Republic operated a parliamentary dual executive where the Head of State (Azikiwe) exercised ceremonial powers and the Head of Government (Balewa) held real executive power.

qs.q: The 1958 Raisman Revenue Allocation Commission in Nigeria was historic because it introduced which specific revenue management mechanism?
o: The State Joint Local Government Account
qs.e: The Raisman Commission created the Distributable Pool Account (DPA) into which specific federally collected duties and mining rents were paid for distribution among regions based on need, population, and balanced development.

qs.q: In the 1953 self-government motion debate in the House of Representatives, Chief Anthony Enahoro of the Action Group moved that Nigeria attain self-government in 1956. The Northern People's Congress (NPC) opposed this motion primarily because
o: The NPC wanted immediate independence in 1953 without delay
The British colonial government threatened to dissolve the Northern House of Chiefs
The NCNC had already declared unilateral independence in Calabar
The North felt administratively and educationally unprepared to compete with the South by 1956
qs.e: Northern leaders felt that due to disparities in Western education and administrative manpower, fixing 1956 as independence date would lead to Southern domination of the federal civil service; they proposed 'as soon as practicable'.

qs.q: The political crisis in the Western Region in 1962 led the Federal Government to declare a state of emergency. Under the Emergency Powers Act 1961, the Federal Government appointed an Administrator for the region who was
qs.e: Following the breakdown of order in the Western House of Assembly in May 1962, Prime Minister Balewa's federal government declared a state of emergency and appointed Dr. M.A. Majekodunmi as Western Region Administrator.

qs.q: Which major pre-independence constitutional conference directly resolved to make Lagos a Federal Territory separate from the Western Region?
qs.e: The 1953 London Conference decided that Lagos, being the chief port and capital, should be carved out of the Western Region and designated as a neutral Federal Territory.

qs.q: In electoral systems, the term 'Duverger's Law' describes the political tendency for single-member district First-Past-The-Post voting systems to favor the emergence of a
qs.e: Duverger's Law is a famous political science generalization stating that single-member district plurality voting (FPTP) naturally leads over time to a dominant two-party system.

qs.q: The United Middle Belt Congress (UMBC), led by Joseph Tarka in the First Republic, functioned primarily as a political party representing
o: Commercial merchant traders in Lagos and Ibadan demanding port deregulation
Traditional Islamic scholars in Kano advocating Sharia state status
Oil-producing communities in the Niger Delta demanding derivation rights
Non-Hausa/Fulani minority ethnic groups in the Northern Region seeking a separate Middle Belt region
qs.e: The UMBC was formed in the 1950s under Joseph Tarka to champion the rights of ethnic minorities in the Middle Belt of Northern Nigeria, allying with the Action Group to demand regional autonomy.

qs.q: During the Second Republic (1979–1983), which political party won the majority of gubernatorial elections and legislative seats in the core Northern states of Kano and Kaduna?
qs.e: The PRP, led by Mallam Aminu Kano, mobilized popular radical anti-feudal support (Talakawa) to win the governorships of both Kano (Abubakar Rimi) and Kaduna (Balarabe Musa) in 1979.

qs.q: A major argument against unicameral legislatures compared to bicameral legislatures in a federal state is that unicameralism
o: Is far more expensive and slow to pass annual appropriation bills
Lacks a second chamber to provide equal regional representation and check hasty legislation
Grants absolute veto power to executive military officers
Prevents citizens from registering in local government councils
qs.e: Unicameralism consists of only one chamber, which risks hasty lawmaking and fails to balance popular representation (population-based) with equal regional/state representation offered by a second chamber.

qs.q: Under the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, if the President dies, resigns, or is permanently incapacitated, who constitutionally succeeds to the office of President for the remainder of the term?
o: The Speaker of the House of Representatives
qs.e: Under Section 146 of the 1999 Constitution, the Vice-President automatically assumes the office of President if the President dies, resigns, or is removed from office.

qs.q: The concept of 'separation of powers' was formally conceptualized and popularized by which French political philosopher in his 1748 treatise 'The Spirit of the Laws'?
qs.e: Baron de Montesquieu articulated the theory of separation of powers, arguing that dividing executive, legislative, and judicial branches prevents tyranny and safeguards liberty.

qs.q: The Udoji Public Service Review Commission of 1972–1974 in Nigeria is best remembered in administrative history for recommending
o: A unified grading and salary structure across the public service and massive wage increases
The total privatization of all state-owned public corporations
The abolition of the Civil Service Commission
The conversion of civil servants into political party organizers
qs.e: The Chief Jerome Udoji Commission introduced a Unified Grading and Salary Structure (UGSS) and substantial wage arrears (Udoji awards) aimed at modernizing public service management.

qs.q: Which constitutional body in Nigeria is vested with the power to recommend the appointment and removal of judicial officers to the executive, as well as exercise disciplinary control over judges?
qs.e: The NJC is an executive constitutional body created to safeguard judicial independence by recommending appointments, promotions, and disciplinary sanctions for judicial officers.

qs.q: The African Union (AU) officially replaced the Organization of African Unity (OAU) following the adoption of the Constitutive Act. In which city was the Sirte Declaration proposing this transformation issued in 1999?
qs.e: The Sirte Declaration was adopted on September 9, 1999, in Sirte, Libya, calling for the establishment of the African Union to accelerate integration.

qs.q: Unlike the OAU Charter which strictly prohibited intervention in internal affairs, Article 4(h) of the AU Constitutive Act grants the African Union the right to intervene in a member state in cases of
o: Failure of a member state to balance its statutory annual budget
Boundary realignments between local government councils
Rejection of European Union economic development grants
Grave circumstances, namely war crimes, genocide, and crimes against humanity
qs.e: Article 4(h) of the AU Constitutive Act marks a major departure from the OAU by granting the AU explicit authority to intervene in member states facing genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.

qs.q: In foreign policy analysis, 'Quiet Diplomacy' refers to a strategy where a government achieves diplomatic objectives primarily through
o: Unpublicized, confidential negotiations and direct persuasion behind closed doors
Public media denunciation and economic sanctions
Unilateral military troop deployments along borders
Filing public lawsuits in international commercial tribunals
qs.e: Quiet diplomacy relies on non-confrontational, confidential bilateral discussions without public media grandstanding to resolve delicate international disputes.

qs.q: The 1983 military coup in Nigeria led by Major-General Muhammadu Buhari terminated the Second Republic primarily on grounds of
o: The refusal of President Shagari to create new states in the North
Rampant political corruption, economic mismanagement, and election rigging in 1983
Border conflicts between Nigeria and neighboring Niger Republic
The adoption of a unicameral National Assembly by parliament
qs.e: The December 31, 1983 coup cited severe economic deterioration, political corruption, inflation, and widespread electoral malpractice in the 1983 general elections as justification.

qs.q: Which major constitutional commission in 1980 headed by Dr. Pius Okigbo made recommendations on revenue allocation in Nigeria's Second Republic?
o: Okigbo Presidential Commission on Revenue Allocation
qs.e: The 1980 Okigbo Commission was appointed by President Shehu Shagari to formulate a revenue allocation formula for the Second Republic, proposing allocation ratios between Federal, State, and Local governments.

qs.q: In political philosophy, Thomas Hobbes' concept of the 'State of Nature' describes a hypothetical human condition characterized by
o: Harmonious communal agrarian cooperation without government
A perfect constitutional democracy governed by fundamental rights
A divine social hierarchy ruled by benevolent philosopher kings
Absolute anarchy, insecurity, and life being solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short
qs.e: Hobbes posited in 'Leviathan' that without a powerful central sovereign (Leviathan), human life in the state of nature is perpetual conflict and 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'.

qs.q: Under John Locke's Social Contract theory, citizens surrender part of their natural freedom to the state primarily to guarantee the protection of their
o: Natural rights to life, liberty, and property
Absolute economic equality of wealth distribution
Right to declare unilateral military war against neighbors
Exemption from paying statutory municipal taxes
qs.e: Locke argued that government is created via social contract specifically to protect citizens' inherent natural rights: life, liberty, and estate (property).

qs.q: A core feature of Karl Marx's theory of Historical Materialism is that all political institutions, legal systems, and ideologies in society are determined by the underlying
o: Religious doctrines of the ruling monarch
Economic structure and mode of production
Military technology available to state general staff
qs.e: Marxist theory holds that the economic base (mode of production and class relations) determines the legal, political, and ideological superstructure of society.

qs.q: A major distinction between a Confederal system and a Federal system is that in a Confederation
o: The central government possesses absolute power while states have no constitutional status
The head of state is automatically an hereditary absolute monarch
The central authority is weak and derives its power entirely from autonomous sovereign member states
Judicial decisions of local councils cannot be appealed to higher courts
qs.e: In a confederation, sovereign states retain ultimate sovereignty and delegate limited powers to a weak central authority, whereas in a federation, sovereignty is shared and the center has direct authority over citizens.

qs.q: Which legal remedy is sought by a litigant asking a superior court to prohibit an inferior administrative tribunal from exceeding its statutory jurisdiction?
qs.e: A Writ of Prohibition prevents a lower court or administrative body from proceeding with a matter outside its legal authority (acting ultra vires).

qs.q: When a court issues a Writ of Mandamus, it is issuing a judicial command compelling a public officer or official body to
o: Perform a mandatory statutory public duty required by law
Vacate a public office obtained through fraudulent election
Surrender all personal assets to the federal treasury
Cease all legislative debates on constitutional amendments
qs.e: Mandamus is an order issued by a court compelling a public officer or administrative body to perform a specific duty that they are legally obligated to perform.

qs.q: In a presidential democracy, if the National Assembly passes a bill and the President takes no action (neither signs nor vetoes) within thirty days, what is the constitutional mechanism under Section 58 of the 1999 Nigerian Constitution?
o: The bill automatically becomes law on the 31st day without presidential assent
The bill can become law if repassed by a two-thirds majority in both houses of the National Assembly
The bill is permanently voided and cannot be reintroduced for four years
The Supreme Court automatically assumes power to sign the bill
qs.e: Under Section 58(5) of the 1999 Constitution, if the President withholding assent fails to sign within 30 days, the bill can be passed into law by a two-thirds supermajority override in both Senate and House.

qs.q: The power of the legislature to remove a sitting Governor or President for 'gross misconduct' in the performance of constitutional functions is called
qs.e: Impeachment is the formal constitutional process by which a legislative body charges and removes a high executive official for gross misconduct.

qs.q: In legislative procedure, a Joint Finance Committee comprising equal members from both the Senate and House of Representatives is convened primarily to
o: Audit the personal bank accounts of Supreme Court justices
Screen foreign ambassadorial appointments submitted by the President
Conduct general elections for local government chairmen
Reconcile conflicting amendments in budget bills passed in different forms by the two chambers
qs.e: A Joint Harmonization or Conference Committee is set up to resolve differences when the two legislative houses pass different versions of the same money/appropriation bill.

qs.q: The practice of 'delegated legislation' is often criticized by political analysts because it
o: Transfers law-making authority to unelected civil servants and executive bodies, eroding parliamentary supremacy
Prevents executive agencies from issuing emergency administrative orders
Requires every administrative rule to be voted on by national referendum
Abolishes judicial review of executive regulations
qs.e: Delegated legislation allows non-elected administrative officials to draft binding regulations, which critics argue circumvents direct legislative scrutiny and democratic representation.

qs.q: Which court in Nigeria possesses exclusive original jurisdiction to hear and determine petitions challenging the election of a person to the office of President or Vice-President?
qs.e: Under Section 239 of the 1999 Constitution, the Court of Appeal acts as the Presidential Election Petition Tribunal with exclusive original jurisdiction over presidential election disputes.

qs.q: A fundamental characteristic of intergovernmental relations in a federal state is that lower tiers of government possess
o: Total immunity from federal tax compliance laws
The right to issue independent national currencies
Constitutionally guaranteed powers that cannot be arbitrarily abolished by the central government
Exemption from all federal High Court appellate rulings
qs.e: Federalism guarantees that state/regional governments derive authority directly from the constitution, preventing central government from unilaterally dismantling them.

qs.q: The 1951 Macpherson Constitution was notable for introducing 'semi-responsible government' at the central level. This meant that Nigerian ministers
o: Held absolute executive power over British colonial governors
Could enact military decrees without parliamentary debates
Were elected directly through national universal adult suffrage
Were appointed to executive portfolios but were individually accountable to regional legislatures and lacked full ministerial control over departments
qs.e: Under Macpherson's 1951 Constitution, Nigerian ministers were given responsibility for government business in the House of Representatives but lacked executive directional control over departments.

qs.q: In the 1964 Federal Elections, the political alliance formed between the Action Group (AG), NCNC, United Middle Belt Congress (UMBC), and Northern Elements Progressive Union (NEPU) was known as the
qs.e: UPGA was formed in 1964 as a broad opposition alliance comprising UPGA (NCNC, AG, UMBC, NEPU) to challenge the ruling NPC-led alliance (NNA) in the 1964 general elections.

qs.q: The opposing political alliance in the 1964 elections, formed by the Northern People's Congress (NPC) and Chief Samuel Akintola's Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP), was the
qs.e: The NNA was formed in 1964 by the ruling NPC and Akintola's breakaway Western NNDP to contest the 1964 election against UPGA.

qs.q: The technique where a pressure group instructs its members to deliberately refuse to purchase goods or services from a targeted corporation to force policy changes is known as a
qs.e: A boycott is an organized commercial strike where consumers or union members collectively abstain from buying or using goods/services to exert financial leverage.

qs.q: In electoral systems, an open-list proportional representation system allows voters to choose
o: Only the party name while the party leadership fixes candidate ranking in secret
Which military general should head the electoral commission
Whether local government elections should be held annually
Individual candidates within a political party list, determining candidate ranking for seat distribution
qs.e: Under open-list proportional representation, voters vote for preferred individual candidates on party lists, directly influencing which candidates fill the seats won by the party.

qs.q: A major objective of the 1988 Dotun Philips Civil Service Reforms was to align civil service management with presidential democracy by making the Minister
o: The Chief Executive and Accounting Officer of the ministry
A permanent career official immune from legislative removal
An ex-officio judge of the Federal High Court
The chairman of the Civil Service Commission
qs.e: The 1988 reform made ministers (rather than Permanent Secretaries) the Chief Executive and Accounting Officers of their ministries, increasing political accountability.

qs.q: Public corporations in Nigeria (such as the Nigerian Railway Corporation) are subjected to legislative control primarily through
o: Direct daily operational management by legislative committee clerks
Parliamentary debate on annual reports, ministerial budget scrutiny, and Public Accounts Committee audits
Unilateral dismissal of lower-level staff by the Senate President
Mandatory annual local government referendums on tariffs
qs.e: Legislative control over public corporations is exercised via committee oversight, approval of budgetary allocations, examination of audited accounts, and statutory debates.

qs.q: Under the 1999 Constitution, local government councils can be dissolved before the expiration of their tenure only in accordance with laws enacted by the
qs.e: Section 7 of the 1999 Constitution mandates State Houses of Assembly to enact laws governing the establishment, structure, tenure, and finance of local government councils.

qs.q: A person who acquires Nigerian citizenship by naturalization may be deprived of that citizenship by the President if the individual
o: Fails to contest elective office in local government elections
Joins a registered trade union or associational pressure group
Criticizes executive economic policies in national newspapers
Acts disloyally towards the Federal Republic or trades with an enemy nation during war
qs.e: Under Section 30 of the 1999 Constitution, the President can revoke naturalization for acts of disloyalty, treasonable conduct, or trading with an enemy state during armed conflict.

qs.q: Nigeria's bold stance against the apartheid regime in South Africa during the Murtala/Obasanjo regime (1975–1979) was highlighted by which major economic action?
o: Nationalizing British Petroleum (BP) assets and Barclays Bank in Nigeria
Withdrawing from the United Nations General Assembly permanently
Imposing oil embargoes on all West African neighboring states
Expelling all diplomatic envoys from the Organization of African Unity
qs.e: Nigeria nationalized British Petroleum (BP) and Barclays Bank assets in 1979 to penalize the UK government for selling oil to apartheid South Africa and failing to enforce sanctions.

qs.q: The Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) brings together leaders of Commonwealth nations every two years to reach decisions based on
o: Veto power held by the British Monarch
Binding two-thirds majority voting in the UN Security Council
Proportional vote weight based on national GDP
qs.e: CHOGM operates on the principle of consensus rather than voting; all member states have equal voice regardless of size or economic wealth.

qs.q: The July 29, 1966 counter-coup in Nigeria was spearheaded primarily by Northern military officers who were motivated by
o: The desire to establish an Islamic Sharia state across Southern Nigeria
Rejection of the 1963 Republican Constitution's creation of Mid-Western region
Grievances over the killings of Northern leaders in January 1966 and opposition to Decree No. 34
A demand to transfer the federal capital from Lagos to Abuja immediately
qs.e: The July 1966 counter-coup arose from Northern anger over the selective assassinations of Northern leaders in January 1966 and General Ironsi's unification decree (Decree 34).

qs.q: Which principle of political culture explains why citizens in some traditional rural agrarian communities have virtually no awareness of central state governance institutions?
qs.e: In a parochial political culture, citizens have low or zero orientation toward central political systems and expect nothing from national institutions, identifying only with local tribes.

qs.q: The doctrine of Social Darwinism when applied to 19th-century political ideology was used primarily by colonial powers to justify
o: Imperial expansion and colonial subjugation of less developed societies
The abolition of private capital ownership
The creation of international judicial arbitration bodies
qs.e: Social Darwinism misapplied 'survival of the fittest' to human societies to justify European imperial conquest and racial subjugation as natural historical evolution.

qs.q: A major distinction between a written constitution and an unwritten constitution is that a written constitution is always
o: Flexible and easily amended by simple legislative resolutions
Embodied in a single comprehensive legal document drafted and adopted at a specific point in time
Derived entirely from unwritten judicial customs and conventions
Subject to automatic renewal every four years by executive decree
qs.e: A written constitution is a single, codified document created by a constituent assembly or constitutional convention, serving as supreme law.

qs.q: According to A.V. Dicey, the Rule of Law is undermined when administrative authorities are granted wide discretionary powers because wide discretion frequently leads to
o: Immediate dissolution of the National Assembly
Automatic repeal of all written criminal codes
Arbitrary exercise of power and unequal treatment of citizens
Compulsory military conscription of civil servants
qs.e: Dicey warned that wide discretionary administrative power leads to arbitrary decisions, undermining legal certainty and equality before the law.

qs.q: In parliamentary systems, the doctrine of 'collective responsibility' dictates that cabinet ministers must
o: Personally pay for budget overruns incurred by their departments
Submit to annual electoral recall petitions by constituents
Refuse to appear before legislative auditing committees
Publicly support all government decisions or resign from cabinet if they disagree
qs.e: Collective responsibility requires all cabinet members to publicly defend decisions made by cabinet; a minister who cannot support a decision must resign.

qs.q: The term 'guillotine motion' in legislative procedure refers to an executive or legislative motion designed to
o: Set a strict time limit on debate for various clauses of a bill to ensure a fast vote
Impeach the Chief Justice of Nigeria for judicial misconduct
Abolish the salary structure of local government chairmen
Suspend constitutional human rights during civil unrest
qs.e: A guillotine (or allocation of time) motion sets strict deadlines for completing debate on stages of a bill, cutting off further discussion when time expires.

qs.q: In public administration, delegated legislation in the form of 'Orders in Council' is issued by the
o: President of the Senate acting alone without executive consultation
Executive acting through the Head of State or Cabinet under statutory authority
Federal High Court when settling land tenure disputes
Chairman of the Federal Character Commission during general elections
qs.e: Orders in Council are executive orders issued by the formal executive (Head of State/Cabinet) pursuant to power delegated by parliamentary statute.

qs.q: The prerogative power of judicial review in Nigeria was famously upheld in the landmark case of Attorney General of Bendel State v. Attorney General of the Federation (1981), where the Supreme Court invalidated the Revenue Allocation Act because
o: The President signed the bill outside the geographical boundaries of Nigeria
The Governor of Bendel State refused to attend the State House of Assembly
The National Assembly failed to follow the mandatory constitutional legislative procedure required for passing money bills
The bill was drafted in English rather than local indigenous languages
qs.e: In AG Bendel State v. AG Federation (1981), the Supreme Court struck down the 1981 Allocation of Revenue Act because the National Assembly breached constitutional law-making procedure.

qs.q: Which commission recommended the establishment of the 'Special Constabulary' and local police forces in minority areas prior to Nigerian independence?
qs.e: The 1958 Willink Commission addressed minority fears by recommending non-discriminatory policing, national fundamental rights guarantees, and special development boards.

qs.q: The Northern Elements Progressive Union (NEPU), founded by Mallam Aminu Kano in 1950, positioned itself ideologically as a radical party advocating the
o: Emancipation of the poor masses (Talakawa) from feudal oppression and aristocratic rule in Northern Nigeria
Creation of an independent oil-producing sovereign state in the South
Immediate unification of Nigeria with the French West African colonies
Establishment of an absolute hereditary monarchy across the Middle Belt
qs.e: NEPU was a radical populist party that challenged traditional feudal aristocracy (Emirs/NPC) in Northern Nigeria, fighting for the political and social rights of the Talakawa.

qs.q: Which pressure group technique involves public demonstrations, peaceful marches, and distribution of handbills outside government headquarters to mobilize public opinion?
qs.e: Picketing is a public demonstration method where protesters gather outside workplaces or government buildings to draw public attention and apply pressure.

qs.q: Under the Single Transferable Vote (STV) system of proportional representation, voters rank candidates in multi-member constituencies using
o: A single checkmark next to the political party logo only
A compulsory oral declaration before the returning officer
Preferential numbers (1, 2, 3...) on the ballot paper
A binary yes/no vote on executive decrees
qs.e: STV is a preferential voting system in multi-member districts where voters rank candidates in order of preference (1st choice, 2nd choice, etc.).

qs.q: The concept of 'Bureaucracy' as an ideal administrative organization characterized by hierarchy, rules, impersonality, and technical competence was formulated by
qs.e: German sociologist Max Weber defined the classic model of bureaucracy based on rational-legal authority, specialization, hierarchy, and strict rules.

qs.q: The General Orders (now Public Service Rules) in the Nigerian Civil Service serve primarily as the
o: Codified administrative rules governing conditions of service, discipline, and conduct of civil servants
Statutory penal code enforced by federal military tribunals
Financial guidelines for state government local council elections
Standing orders of the House of Representatives during budget debates
qs.e: Public Service Rules (formerly General Orders) set out regulatory conditions of service, operational procedures, and ethical standards for civil servants.

qs.q: Under the 1999 Constitution, local government councils derive their statutory financial allocation from the Federation Account through the
qs.e: Under Section 162(6) of the 1999 Constitution, federal funds allocated to local governments in a state are paid into the State Joint Local Government Account.

qs.q: Which constitutional right guaranteed under Chapter IV of the 1999 Nigerian Constitution protects citizens against arbitrary arrest and unlawful detention by state security agencies?
o: Right to freedom of thought and conscience
Right to peaceful assembly and association
qs.e: Section 35 guarantees the Right to Personal Liberty, stipulating that no person shall be deprived of liberty except in accordance with procedures permitted by law.

qs.q: Nigeria's leadership role in establishing the Technical Aid Corps (TAC) scheme in 1987 under General Ibrahim Babangida was designed to
o: Deploy active military officers to enforce border controls across West Africa
Export raw crude oil at discounted prices to European Union countries
Establish offshore financial intelligence centers in Latin America
Provide Nigerian skilled manpower and technical assistance to developing African, Caribbean, and Pacific (ACP) nations
qs.e: The TAC scheme, launched in 1987, deploys young Nigerian professionals (doctors, teachers, engineers) to ACP countries as a tool of soft power and Afrocentric foreign assistance.

qs.q: The United Nations General Assembly decisions on important international questions (such as peace recommendations or budget approvals) require a
o: Two-thirds majority of members present and voting
Unanimous vote of all member states
Simple majority vote of the 5 permanent Security Council members
Consensus approval from the International Court of Justice
qs.e: Under Article 18 of the UN Charter, decisions on important questions in the General Assembly require a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.

qs.q: The 1975 military coup that removed General Yakubu Gowon from power occurred while Gowon was attending an OAU Summit in Kampala. The coup leaders appointed as Head of State
qs.e: On July 29, 1975, General Gowon was overthrown in a bloodless coup while attending the OAU Summit, and Brigadier Murtala Muhammed became Head of State.

qs.q: The concept of 'rule by divine right' was historically used in political monarchies to claim that
o: Power resides exclusively in the elected representatives of the working class
The judiciary holds supreme veto power over royal succession decrees
The monarch derives political authority directly from God and is accountable to no earthly parliament
Local government councils must be elected through direct secret ballot
qs.e: The Divine Right of Kings asserted that monarchs derive sovereign authority directly from God, making royal decisions immune to earthly accountability.

qs.q: A core principle of Classical Liberalism is the belief in
o: Total state ownership of all industrial factories and land
The divine rule of traditional hereditary chiefs
Enforcing mandatory state religious doctrines through criminal courts
Minimal state intervention in individual economic activity and maximum personal liberty
qs.e: Classical liberalism emphasizes individual freedom, private property, free markets, and limited government interference in economic and personal life.

qs.q: The principle of 'constitutionalism' means that government power must be
o: Limited and bound by explicit constitutional rules and legal procedures
Vested entirely in a single military supreme commander during peace
Exercised without any possibility of judicial challenge in court
Derived strictly from decrees issued by regional traditional rulers
qs.e: Constitutionalism is the principle that government authority is derived from and limited by a supreme constitution, preventing arbitrary or tyrannical governance.

qs.q: Which legal document historically laid the foundation for civil liberties and limited royal absolutism in England in 1215?
qs.e: The Magna Carta (1215) forced King John to accept legal limits on royal power, laying early foundations for the Rule of Law and constitutional government.

qs.q: In a parliamentary system, if the executive branch dissolves parliament and calls early general elections, this action is taken by the Head of State on the advice of the
qs.e: In parliamentary governance, the Prime Minister has the constitutional prerogative to request the Head of State to dissolve parliament and trigger snap general elections.

qs.q: The legislative power to investigate financial corruption or maladministration in government ministries through special probe committees is called the power of
qs.e: Under Sections 88 and 89 of the 1999 Constitution, the legislature holds investigative powers to inquire into public funds and expose corruption or inefficiency.

qs.q: The principle of 'fiscal federalism' deals primarily with the constitutional arrangements governing
o: The allocation of revenue-raising powers and expenditure responsibilities between tiers of government
The deployment of military forces during regional civil disturbances
The appointment of international judges to regional economic tribunals
The registration of political parties by central electoral commissions
qs.e: Fiscal federalism addresses financial relationships, revenue assignment, tax jurisdictions, and statutory transfers among different tiers of a federal government.

qs.q: The 1960 Independence Constitution of Nigeria differed from the 1963 Republican Constitution primarily because under the 1960 Constitution
o: The Supreme Court of Nigeria was the court of last resort
The Queen of England remained Nigeria's titular Head of State represented by a Governor-General
The President exercised absolute executive powers without a Prime Minister
Nigeria operated a unicameral central parliament in Lagos
qs.e: Under the 1960 Independence Constitution, Queen Elizabeth II was retained as Head of State (represented locally by Governor-General Azikiwe) until the 1963 Republican transition.

qs.q: The National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC), formed in 1944 with Herbert Macaulay as President and Nnamdi Azikiwe as Secretary-General, was historically significant as a
o: Regional political party representing Western cocoa farmers exclusively
Pro-colonial advisory council organized by the British Governor
Vibrant nationwide nationalist movement seeking self-governance for Nigeria
Traditional religious movement in Northern Nigeria
qs.e: The NCNC was Nigeria's first major nationalist party with broad nationwide cross-regional membership, leading anti-colonial agitation across the country.

qs.q: In pressure group terminology, 'hyper-pluralism' describes a situation where
o: The government bans all non-governmental associations nationwide
Political parties merge into a single official state party
Local government councils operate without statutory budgets
So many competing pressure groups become powerful that government policy becomes gridlocked and contradictory
qs.e: Hyper-pluralism occurs when interest groups become so strong and numerous that government attempts to satisfy all of them, resulting in contradictory policies and political paralysis.

qs.q: The electoral system where voters cast a single vote for a party list, and candidates win seats strictly in the order they appear on the list, is called
qs.e: In closed-list proportional representation, political party leadership fixes candidate rankings on party lists, and voters cannot alter the order of candidates.

qs.q: The United Nations Security Council consists of fifteen member states. The five permanent members possessing absolute veto power over non-procedural resolutions are
o: United States, Germany, Japan, India, and Brazil
United States, United Kingdom, France, Russia, and China
United Kingdom, France, Germany, China, and South Africa
Russia, China, India, Nigeria, and Canada
qs.e: The P5 permanent members of the UN Security Council established in 1945 are the United States, United Kingdom, France, Russia (formerly USSR), and China.

qs.q: <svg width="300" height="150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#fff;"><rect x="100" y="10" width="100" height="35" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150" y="32" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif">Federal Level</text><rect x="20" y="80" width="80" height="35" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/><text x="60" y="102" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif">Exclusive</text><rect x="110" y="80" width="80" height="35" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150" y="102" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif">Concurrent</text><rect x="200" y="80" width="80" height="35" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/><text x="240" y="102" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif">Residual</text><path d="M 150 45 L 60 80 M 150 45 L 150 80 M 150 45 L 240 80" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/></svg> Referring to the federal power structure tree in the diagram, if a new emerging technology arises that is omitted from both the Exclusive and Concurrent lists, which level of government holds constitutional authority over it?
o: Federal Government under implied exclusive powers
Local Government Councils under customary municipal powers
State Governments under residual legislative powers
Federal Executive Council by issuing administrative decrees
qs.e: Under federal constitutional jurisprudence, any legislative subject omitted from both the Exclusive and Concurrent lists automatically falls under the Residual List, which belongs exclusively to State Houses of Assembly.

qs.q: The landmark Supreme Court judgment in Attorney General of the Federation v. Attorney General of Abia State & Ors (2002) regarding the Off-Shore/On-Shore Dichotomy established that
o: Littoral states hold absolute ownership of all natural gas deposits up to 200 nautical miles into the continental shelf
Derivation funds must be paid directly to local government traditional councils rather than state treasuries
The Federal Government has no constitutional authority to levy customs duties on maritime imports
The seaward boundary of a littoral state extends only to the low-water mark, making off-shore natural resources federal property
qs.e: The Supreme Court ruled in 2002 that the southern boundaries of littoral states end at the low-water mark, vesting off-shore territorial waters and continental shelf resources exclusively in the Federal Government.

qs.q: Under Section 308 of the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, the executive immunity clause protects the President, Vice-President, Governors, and Deputy Governors from
o: Civil or criminal court proceedings and arrest during their tenure of office
Legislative impeachment probes initiated by the House of Assembly
Audits conducted by the Auditor-General of the Federation
Internal party disciplinary actions and expulsion
qs.e: Section 308 grants absolute constitutional immunity from civil or criminal court summons, prosecution, or arrest to incumbents of executive offices (President, VP, Governors, Deputy Governors) while in office.

qs.q: In the controversial 1979 Presidential Election dispute (Awolowo v. Shagari), the central legal question hinged on the mathematical interpretation of 'two-thirds of 19 states'. The Supreme Court upheld the election of Shehu Shagari by ruling that two-thirds of 19 states meant
o: 13 whole states rounded up to the nearest integer
12 states plus two-thirds of the votes cast in the 13th state (Kano State)
12 whole states without any fractional calculation
qs.e: The Supreme Court accepted the technical submission that two-thirds of 19 is 12 and 2/3, holding that FEDECO correctly declared Shagari elected since he met 25% in 12 states plus over 25% of 2/3 of votes in Kano State.

qs.q: The Mid-Western Region was created in August 1963 following a plebiscite and constitutional procedure. What made this state creation historically unique in Nigerian political history?
o: It was created via a military decree issued by the Supreme Military Council
It was formed by merging two Northern emirates with Lagos Federal Territory
It was the only region ever created strictly through democratic civilian constitutional process
It abolished the post of regional Premier and House of Chiefs
qs.e: Mid-Western Region was carved out of the Western Region in 1963 pursuant to Section 4 of the 1960/1963 Constitution, making it the only region created through peaceful civilian constitutional mechanics.

qs.q: Under the 1979 and 1999 Constitutions of Nigeria, the Federal Character Commission was established to ensure that
o: All registered political parties maintain identical campaign manifestos
The President selects ministers strictly from the military officer corps
Local government councils operate without central budgetary allocations
Appointments to public federal agencies reflect equitably the linguistic, ethnic, and geographic diversity of Nigeria
qs.e: The Federal Character Commission enforces the constitutional mandate (Section 14(3)) ensuring fair and equitable distribution of public posts and socio-economic infrastructure across all federating units.

qs.q: The 1988 Dotun Philips Civil Service Reform attempted to abolish which traditional administrative body and replace it with internal ministry personnel boards?
o: The traditional centralized Civil Service Commission recruitment role for middle cadres
The Public Accounts Committee of the House of Representatives
The Federal Character Commission monitoring unit
The National Judicial Council recommendation tribunal
qs.e: The 1988 reform decentralized staff recruitment, promotion, and discipline directly to individual ministries (under Ministerial Personnel Boards), undermining the traditional Civil Service Commission authority.

qs.q: In historical revenue allocation, the Hicks-Phillipson Commission of 1951 recommended four principles for sharing national revenue among regions. Which of the following was one of those principles?
o: Off-shore Exploration, Landmass, Terrain, and Population Density
Derivation, Need, National Interest, and Independent Revenue
Internal Tax Capacity, Inflation Rate, Foreign Reserve, and Trade Deficit
Military Budget, Judicial Salaries, Chieftaincy Stipends, and Port Tariff
qs.e: The 1951 Hicks-Phillipson Commission proposed four primary criteria: Derivation, Need, National Interest, and Continuity/Independent Revenue.

qs.q: During the 1993 transition program under General Ibrahim Babangida, the federal military government instituted a compulsory two-party framework. The two state-created political parties were the
o: People's Democratic Party (PDP) and All Progressives Congress (APC)
Unity Party of Nigeria (UPN) and National Party of Nigeria (NPN)
Social Democratic Party (SDP) and National Republican Convention (NRC)
Nigerian National Alliance (NNA) and United Progressive Grand Alliance (UPGA)
qs.e: Babangida's military regime established two grassroots political parties by decree: the SDP ('a little to the left') and the NRC ('a little to the right').

qs.q: The annulment of the June 12, 1993 presidential election (won by Chief M.K.O. Abiola) led to the resignation of General Babangida and the installation of an Interim National Government (ING) headed by
qs.e: Following intense public outrage over the June 12 annulment, General Babangida stepped aside in August 1993, appointing Chief Ernest Shonekan to head the short-lived Interim National Government.

qs.q: In November 1993, the Interim National Government led by Ernest Shonekan was declared illegal by a High Court judgment delivered by Justice Dolapo Akinsanya. Shortly after, the ING was overthrown by
qs.e: On November 17, 1993, General Sani Abacha forced Ernest Shonekan to resign, dissolved all democratic institutions, and established the Provisional Ruling Council (PRC).

qs.q: The Bakassi Peninsula border dispute between Nigeria and Cameroon was formally brought before the International Court of Justice (ICJ). In October 2002, the ICJ ruled in favor of Cameroon primarily based on the
qs.e: The ICJ awarded sovereignty over Bakassi to Cameroon in October 2002 based on the 1913 Anglo-German treaty, leading to the 2006 Greentree Agreement and peaceful transfer.

qs.q: Which international trade and economic agreement signed in 1975 established trade preferences between European Union nations and developing ACP (African, Caribbean, and Pacific) countries?
qs.e: The Lomé Convention (first signed in Lomé, Togo in 1975) established non-reciprocal trade preferences and aid frameworks between the European Economic Community and ACP states.

qs.q: Under the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, a proposed amendment affecting fundamental human rights or state creation requires a special legislative threshold in the National Assembly of
o: Simple majority of members present and voting in a joint sitting
Two-thirds majority in Senate and simple majority in House of Representatives
Unanimous approval by the Federal Executive Council and Council of State
Four-fifths majority of all members of each house and approval by two-thirds of State Houses of Assembly
qs.e: Section 9(3) specifies that amending Section 8 (state creation/boundary adjustment) or Chapter IV (fundamental rights) requires an elevated four-fifths supermajority in both National Assembly houses plus approval by two-thirds of State Assemblies.

qs.q: The concept of 'Monism' in international law holds that international treaties signed and ratified by a state automatically become part of domestic national law. In contrast, Nigeria practices 'Dualism' (Section 12 of 1999 Constitution), meaning an international treaty
o: Has no force of law domestically unless enacted into law by the National Assembly
Is automatically superior to the 1999 Constitution upon executive signature
Must be approved by a national referendum before diplomatic signature
Applies strictly inside Federal Capital Territory Abuja
qs.e: Under Section 12 of the 1999 Constitution (Dualist doctrine), no international treaty or accord signed by the executive has force of law in Nigeria until the National Assembly enacts it into domestic statute.

qs.q: In the 1951 Macpherson Constitution, the central legislative body was called the House of Representatives. Members of this central house were selected through
o: Direct universal adult suffrage across all federal constituencies
Indirect election from the Regional Houses of Assembly acting as electoral colleges
Direct appointment by the British Colonial Secretary in London
Ex-officio nomination by traditional Emirs and Obas
qs.e: Under Macpherson's 1951 framework, members of the central House of Representatives were elected indirectly from among members of the Regional Houses of Assembly (acting as electoral colleges).

qs.q: The Mbanefo Salary Commission (1959) and Morgan Commission (1964) in Nigerian public administration were instituted primarily to address grievances regarding
o: The abolition of regional civil service recruitment boards
The nationalization of foreign commercial banks
Wage disparities, inflation, and public sector minimum wage adjustments
The re-alignment of local government council electoral boundaries
qs.e: These commissions evaluated public sector living standards, cost-of-living allowances, and minimum wage demands to resolve industrial agitation.

qs.q: The 1976 Local Government Reforms prescribed a specific demographic population threshold for establishing a standard Local Government Area in Nigeria. What was this range?
qs.e: The 1976 Reform Guidelines stipulated that a local government area should ideally cover a population between 150,000 and 800,000 to ensure administrative viability.

qs.q: In political science, the 'Iron Law of Oligarchy', formulated by sociologist Robert Michels, posits that
o: All complex organizations, regardless of how democratic they appear, inevitably develop leadership elites who dominate decision-making
Military regimes in developing nations automatically transition to stable multi-party democracies within five years
Proportional representation electoral systems eliminate all political corruption
Unwritten constitutions guarantee greater personal freedom than written constitutions
qs.e: Robert Michels argued that democratic organizations naturally succumb to elite control because organizational complexity requires specialized leadership, concentrating power in a few hands.

qs.q: Under the doctrine of parliamentary supremacy in the United Kingdom, parliament can enact or repeal any law whatsoever. In contrast, in Nigeria's constitutional democracy, supremacy resides in the
o: Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria
qs.e: Under Section 1(1) of the 1999 Constitution, the Constitution is supreme and its provisions bind all authorities and persons throughout Nigeria.

qs.q: The principle of 'Quo Warranto' is an extraordinary legal remedy issued by a superior court to
o: Force the President to sign an appropriation bill within 24 hours
Transfer a criminal murder trial from a State High Court to a Customary Court
Inquire by what legal authority an individual holds or exercises a public office or franchise
Order local government councils to lower market stall fees
qs.e: Quo Warranto ('by what warrant') challenges an individual who usurps or improperly holds a public office to demonstrate their legal authority to occupy that position.

qs.q: When the British colonial administration applied 'Indirect Rule' in Northern Nigeria through Lord Lugard, it utilized traditional native authorities. Why did Indirect Rule face severe operational failure when extended to Eastern Nigeria?
o: The Eastern Region possessed a highly developed industrial working class that rejected traditional chiefs
The British colonial office refused to fund warrant chiefs in Calabar
Islamic Sharia courts resisted the jurisdiction of British district officers
The Igbo society was traditionally decentralized and acephalous, lacking centralized hereditary monarchs
qs.e: Igbo political organization was republican and acephalous (decentralized). Imposing artificial 'Warrant Chiefs' created intense popular resentment, culminating in events like the 1929 Aba Women's War.

qs.q: The Aba Women's War of 1929 in Eastern Nigeria was triggered primarily by fears that the British colonial administration intended to
o: Extend direct taxation to women under the Warrant Chief system
Abolish Christianity and enforce traditional idol worship
Transfer palm oil plantations to Northern emirate rulers
Draft Igbo youth into the British Royal Navy
qs.e: The 1929 Aba Women's War was a major anti-colonial revolt sparked by census enumerations conducted by Warrant Chiefs, which women believed was a prelude to direct taxation.

qs.q: In the First Republic, the Action Group crisis of 1962 resulted from an intense ideological and personal rift between Chief Obafemi Awolowo and
qs.e: The 1962 AG crisis stemmed from tactical and ideological disagreements between party leader Awolowo (advocating democratic socialism and firm opposition) and Premier Akintola (advocating joining the federal ruling NPC coalition).

qs.q: Which major constitutional feature was introduced in the 1989 Constitution (Third Republic framework) to reduce ethnic polarization in party politics?
o: Abolition of the Senate and creation of a unicameral assembly
Rotational presidency mandated strictly by state origin
