qs.e: The 1960 Independence Constitution retained the British Queen (Elizabeth II) as constitutional Head of State, represented in Nigeria by the Governor-General (Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe), with executive power exercised by Prime Minister Balewa.

qs.q: The Northern People's Congress (NPC) during Nigeria's First Republic was characterized primarily as a
o: Regionally-based party rooted in the northern traditional aristocracies and conservative values
Radical pan-African party advocating immediate national socialist revolution
Southern merchant party focused on cocoa and rubber exports
qs.e: The NPC, led by Sir Ahmadu Bello, drew its main support base from the Northern Region and traditional native authorities, adopting a conservative political ideology encapsulated in its motto 'One North, One People'.

qs.q: Which of the following is an example of an associational pressure group in Nigeria?
o: Movement for the Survival of the Ogoni People (MOSOP)
qs.e: Associational pressure groups are formally organized groups formed specifically to represent the professional or economic interests of their members (e.g. NMA, NBA, ASUU, NLC).

qs.q: To be declared winner of a presidential election in Nigeria under the 1999 Constitution, a candidate must win the highest number of votes AND
o: At least 25% of the votes cast in at least two-thirds of all the States and the FCT
An absolute majority of 75% of all registered voters nationwide
A simple majority in every single state of the federation
Two-thirds of all seats in the National Assembly
qs.e: Section 133/134 of the 1999 Constitution mandates that a presidential candidate must win the highest total votes AND secure at least 25% of votes in at least two-thirds of the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

qs.q: The fundamental difference between privatization and commercialization of state-owned enterprises is that privatization involves
o: Selling state equity/ownership to private investors, whereas commercialization retains state ownership but mandates profit-oriented management
Transferring ownership to foreign governments, while commercialization hands assets to local councils
Abolishing all tariffs and fees for consumers, while commercialization doubles utility prices
Converting statutory boards into military command centers
qs.e: Privatization transfers ownership/control of state assets to private entities. Commercialization retains government ownership but requires the enterprise to operate efficiently on commercial, profit-making principles.

qs.q: The constitutional body responsible for recruiting, promoting, and disciplining junior and senior staff in federal government ministries is the
qs.e: The Federal Civil Service Commission (FCSC) is executive body tasked with setting guidelines for recruitment, appointment, promotion, and discipline within the federal civil service.

qs.q: Following the 1976 Local Government Reforms in Nigeria, traditional rulers were
o: Insulated from executive local administration and given advisory roles in Traditional Councils
Made executive chairmen of local government councils nationwide
Granted exclusive powers to collect federal import duties
Appointed as presiding judges over state high courts
qs.e: The 1976 reforms separated traditional chieftaincy institutions from democratic local government structures, placing traditional rulers in advisory Emirate or Traditional Councils without executive political powers.

qs.q: In African political thought, Communitarianism emphasizes that individual rights and identities are
o: Embedded within and subordinate to the well-being and solidarity of the community
Completely independent of societal relationships and cultural obligations
Derived exclusively from written statutes enacted by colonial parliaments
Secondary to the unlimited accumulation of personal capitalist wealth
qs.e: Communitarianism holds that individuals are fundamentally social beings whose identity and duties are shaped by their community, prioritizing collective harmony and shared social responsibilities.

qs.q: In unwritten constitutional systems like the United Kingdom, constitutional conventions are best described as
o: Non-legal binding rules of political practice accepted as binding by political actors
Formal written statutes passed by the House of Lords every decade
Decrees issued by the Supreme Court during national emergencies
International trade treaties ratified by referendum
qs.e: Constitutional conventions are unwritten legal practices and customs followed by government actors (e.g. the Monarch giving royal assent to bills) that are politically binding though not enforced by courts.

qs.q: Centrifugal forces in a federal state are those tendencies that
o: Push sub-national units toward regional autonomy, secession, or disintegration
Unify diverse ethnic groups into a centralized unitary government
Strengthen the power of the central president over state governors
Abolish state borders to create a single national administrative zone
qs.e: Centrifugal forces divide a state (such as regional imbalances, ethnic rivalries, or secessionist demands). Centripetal forces draw a nation together toward national unity.

qs.q: The Federal Character Principle was formally enshrined in the 1979 Constitution of Nigeria to solve which major national governance problem?
o: Ethnic and regional domination in federal appointments and government institutions
Hyper-inflation resulting from petroleum price volatility
The breakdown of law and order in local government market councils
The lack of judicial review powers in regional high courts
qs.e: The Federal Character Principle (Section 14(3) of 1999 Constitution, introduced in 1979) was designed to ensure fair representation of all ethnic, regional, and state groups in public appointments and federal agencies to prevent dominance by any single group.

qs.q: The 1953 Motion for Self-Government moved by Chief Anthony Enahoro in the House of Representatives caused a severe political crisis because northern political leaders argued that
o: Self-government in 1956 was premature and proposed replacing '1956' with 'as soon as practicable'
Nigeria should remain a permanent British crown colony indefinitely
The Southern regions should secede from the Nigerian federation immediately
The federal capital should be relocated from Lagos to Kano
qs.e: Northern leaders (NPC) felt the North lacked educated personnel to compete with the South if self-government were granted in 1956. Ibrahim Ahmadu Bello moved an amendment changing the date to 'as soon as practicable', triggering acute inter-regional tensions.

qs.q: When pressure groups use litigation as a strategy, their primary aim is to
o: Challenge the constitutionality or legality of government policies in court to protect member interests
Bribe judicial officers to secure favorable business contracts
Displace elected legislators and assume legislative functions
Delay elections by freezing electoral commission bank accounts
qs.e: Litigation involves bringing test cases or legal challenges before courts to invalidate executive regulations or legislative statutes that infringe upon the rights or interests of interest group members.

qs.q: Why was the Anglo-Nigerian Defence Pact abrogated in 1962?
o: Widespread public protests by university students, trade unions, and nationalist politicians against compromised sovereignty
The British Parliament refused to supply military hardware to Nigeria
Nigeria joined the Warsaw Pact military alliance with the USSR
The Nigerian Supreme Court ruled the pact invalid under colonial law
qs.e: The 1960 Anglo-Nigerian Defence Pact would have allowed Britain to maintain air bases in Nigeria. Intense protests led by student unions (NANS predecessor) and opposition parties forced Prime Minister Balewa to cancel the agreement in 1962.

qs.q: A major criticism of the Organization of African Unity (OAU) Charter was that its strict adherence to non-interference prevented the organization from
o: Intervening effectively in internal civil wars and human rights abuses committed by dictatorial regimes
Establishing a common West African central bank and currency
Admitting newly independent Lusophone African nations
Participating in UN General Assembly debates
qs.e: The OAU Charter's strict clause on non-interference in internal affairs prevented the OAU from acting against notorious dictators (like Idi Amin) or intervening in domestic atrocities, earning it the label of a 'dictators' club'.

qs.q: General Aguiyi-Ironsi's Decree No. 34 of 1966 (Unification Decree) provoked intense political opposition in northern Nigeria because it
o: Abolished the federal system and unified the civil service, raising fears of southern administrative dominance
Created 12 new states out of the existing four regions
Banned all traditional rulers from participating in Emirate councils
Transferred oil revenue allocation exclusively to local councils
qs.e: Decree 34 abolished the regional federal structure and centralized the civil service into a single national framework. Northern elites feared this would allow better-educated southerners to dominate civil service appointments nationwide.

qs.q: General Yakubu Gowon's division of Nigeria into 12 states in May 1967 was a strategic political move designed to
o: Weaken Eastern Region solidarity by granting autonomous states to minority groups prior to secession
Prevent the Western Region from declaring an independent republic
Restore full civilian executive rule within six months
Satisfy demands by traditional rulers for regional autonomy
qs.e: By splitting the Eastern Region into three states (Rivers, South-Eastern, and East Central), Gowon detached non-Igbo minority areas (Rivers and South-Eastern) from the Igbo core, undercutting Ojukwu's Biafran coalition.

qs.q: The institution of the Ombudsman (Public Complaints Commission in Nigeria) serves citizens primarily as a protection against
o: Administrative injustice, bureaucratic harassment, and abuse of office by public officials
Foreign military aggression and territorial invasions
Unlawful commercial price-fixing by private trade cartels
Unconstitutional judicial precedents set by the Supreme Court
qs.e: The Ombudsman investigates complaints of administrative unfairness, corruption, red tape, and official abuse by public servants, providing citizens with a non-judicial avenue for redress.

qs.q: Jean Bodin's theoretical formulation of sovereignty as 'supreme power over citizens and subjects, unrestrained by law' was modified in modern constitutional theory by the principle that
o: Sovereignty resides in the people (popular sovereignty) and is subject to constitutional limitations
Sovereignty belongs exclusively to hereditary monarchs without parliamentary consent
Sovereignty can only be exercised by military ruling councils
International financial institutions possess absolute authority over national constitutions
qs.e: While Bodin viewed sovereignty as absolute and undivided under a sovereign prince, modern constitutionalism posits that sovereignty originates from the people and is constrained by fundamental rights and constitutional checks.

qs.q: The Willink Commission of 1957 was appointed by the British colonial government primarily to
o: Investigate the fears of ethnic minority groups in the regions and recommend safeguards
Determine the exact date for Nigeria's independence from Britain
Draft a new federal constitution replacing the Lyttelton Constitution
Reorganize the Nigerian military command structure
qs.e: The Henry Willink Commission was set up to examine minority anxieties over majority domination in the North (Hausa-Fulani), West (Yoruba), and East (Igbo). The commission recommended adding fundamental rights to the constitution rather than creating new minority states.

qs.q: Nigeria established the Special Nigeria Trust Fund (NTF) at the African Development Bank (AfDB) in 1976 primarily to
o: Provide low-interest concessionary financing to low-income African countries for development projects
Fund Nigerian military operations during West African peacekeeping missions
Bail out European commercial banks facing foreign exchange deficits
Pay for crude oil exploration along the Gulf of Guinea
qs.e: During the 1970s oil boom, Nigeria created the NTF at the AfDB to assist poorer African nations by offering soft, low-interest loans for infrastructure, health, and agricultural development.

qs.q: Within the United Nations administrative system, the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) coordinates the activities of specialized agencies by
o: Receiving reports, issuing policy recommendations, and coordinating economic and social programming
Directing military peacekeeping troops assigned to regional conflicts
Appointing judges to the International Court of Justice in The Hague
Issuing binding trade sanctions against non-member nations
qs.e: ECOSOC is the principal UN organ responsible for coordinating economic, social, cultural, and health initiatives across 15 specialized UN agencies (such as WHO, UNESCO, ILO, and FAO).

qs.q: In electoral mechanics, the Single Transferable Vote (STV) system achieves proportional representation in multi-member districts by requiring voters to
o: Rank candidates in order of preference, transferring surplus votes from winning candidates to voters' lower choices
Vote exclusively for a single political party list without choosing individual candidates
Cast two ballots—one for the constituency representative and one for the national president
Select candidates solely on the basis of political party seniority
qs.e: STV is a preferential voting system in multi-member constituencies where voters rank candidates (1, 2, 3...). Surplus votes beyond the winning quota, or votes for eliminated low-ranking candidates, are transferred to remaining choices.

qs.q:
Examine the federal legislative list diagram below:
<svg width="300" height="110" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#fff;"><rect x="100" y="10" width="100" height="30" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="150" y="28" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">Constitution</text><rect x="10" y="70" width="85" height="30" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="52" y="88" font-size="9" text-anchor="middle">Exclusive List</text><rect x="107" y="70" width="85" height="30" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="150" y="88" font-size="9" text-anchor="middle">Concurrent List</text><rect x="205" y="70" width="85" height="30" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="247" y="88" font-size="9" text-anchor="middle">Residual List</text><path d="M 150 40 L 52 70 M 150 40 L 150 70 M 150 40 L 247 70" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/></svg>
If a conflict arises between a federal law and a state law regarding an item on the Concurrent List, what is the constitutional outcome in Nigeria?
o: The federal law prevails and the state law becomes void to the extent of the inconsistency
The state law automatically overrides the federal law
Both laws are submitted to a popular national referendum
The item is permanently moved to the Residual Legislative List
qs.e: Under Section 4(5) of the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria (Doctrine of Inconsistency), if a law enacted by a State House of Assembly is inconsistent with a law validly made by the National Assembly on a concurrent subject, the federal law prevails and the state law is void to the extent of inconsistency.

qs.q: Which three arms constitute the structure of modern democratic government?
o: Civil Service, Police, and Trade Unions
qs.e: The three classical arms of government in modern political doctrine are the Legislature (makes laws), the Executive (enforces laws), and the Judiciary (interprets laws).

qs.q: The fundamental difference between power and authority is that authority is
o: Legitimate power backed by right and public acceptance, whereas power relies on coercion
Based strictly on military physical force
Held exclusively by private corporate executives
qs.e: Power is the capacity to compel compliance through force or influence. Authority is legitimate power—the recognized, lawful right to command obedience, accepted as proper by those governed.

qs.q: Which of the following is an example of a statutory public corporation in Nigeria?
qs.e: NNPC is a state-owned statutory enterprise created to manage state commercial oil production assets, distinct from civil service government ministries.

qs.q: Foreign nationals seeking Nigerian citizenship through naturalization must fulfill the requirement of
o: Continuous residence in Nigeria for a required constitutional period and proof of good character
Marriage to a state governor or high-ranking minister
Passing a written examination on ancient traditional folklore
Investing 90 percent of their wealth in local real estate
qs.e: Section 27 of the 1999 Constitution lays out naturalization requirements, including continuous residence in Nigeria for 15 years, good character, assimilation into local customs, and taking the oath of allegiance.

qs.q: Universal adult suffrage grants the right to vote in national elections to
o: All qualified adult citizens regardless of property, gender, or social status
Only property-owning male taxpayers over fifty years of age
Educated civil servants holding university degrees
qs.e: Universal adult suffrage means every adult citizen meeting the constitutional age threshold (e.g. 18 years in Nigeria) has the right to vote without discrimination based on wealth, property, gender, or education.

qs.q: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was formally established in 1975 through the signing of the
qs.e: ECOWAS was established on May 28, 1975, with the signing of the Treaty of Lagos by 15 West African states to promote economic integration and regional cooperation.

qs.q: A core political characteristic of Fascism as demonstrated in historical regimes is
o: Totalitarian state control, militant nationalism, and aggressive suppression of opposition
Enforcing multi-party parliamentary elections every four years
Protecting individual civil liberties against state interference
Abolishing standing military forces in favor of local police
qs.e: Fascism is an authoritarian, totalitarian ideology that exalts the nation and state above the individual, relies on dictatorial leadership, suppresses political opposition, and mobilizes society militarily.

qs.q: A flexible constitution can be defined as one whose provisions can be amended by
o: The ordinary lawmaking procedure of the legislature using a simple majority vote
A special constituent assembly approved by national referendum
A two-thirds vote in all sub-national state assemblies
An executive order signed by the Chief Justice
qs.e: A flexible constitution can be altered or amended through the same ordinary legislative process used for passing everyday statutes, without demanding complex supermajorities.

qs.q: Which prerogative judicial writ commands a public officer or government agency to perform a mandatory statutory duty?
qs.e: Mandamus ('we command') is a judicial order issued by a superior court commanding a public official, administrative tribunal, or lower court to perform a specific legal duty required by law.

qs.q: The primary lawmaking function of parliament involves
o: Debating, amending, and enacting statutory bills into law
Directing executive police operations in criminal investigations
Managing day-to-day administrative civil service appointments
Enforcing judicial sentences passed by magistrate courts
qs.e: The primary constitutional duty of the legislature is lawmaking—introducing, debating, scrutinizing, amending, and passing statutory legislation.

qs.q: In a presidential democracy, key executive appointments made by the President (such as ministers and ambassadors) must be confirmed by the
qs.e: To maintain checks and balances, the 1999 Constitution mandates that presidential nominations for ministers, ambassadors, and heads of federal bodies must be confirmed by the Senate before taking office.

qs.q: The hierarchy of regular courts in Nigeria, starting from the intermediate court of record to the apex court, runs from the
o: High Court to Court of Appeal to Supreme Court
Magistrate Court to Customary Court to High Court
Supreme Court to Court of Appeal to High Court
Federal High Court to Industrial Court to Privy Council
qs.e: In the Nigerian judicial hierarchy, appeals move from trial courts of record (High Courts) up to the Court of Appeal, and finally to the Supreme Court.

qs.q: The 1946 Richards Constitution was notable for introducing regionalism into Nigeria by creating regional Houses of Assembly for the
o: Lagos, Calabar, and Port Harcourt Municipalities
Mid-Western, Southern, and Niger Delta Protectorates
qs.e: The Richards Constitution of 1946 formally divided Nigeria into three administrative regions—Northern, Western, and Eastern—and established Regional Houses of Assembly for each.

qs.q: A cadre political party differs from a mass political party because a cadre party
o: Is dominated by a small, highly disciplined group of elites and notable leaders rather than broad popular membership
Recruits millions of ordinary grassroots members across all voting wards
Avoids contesting parliamentary or local elections
Operates exclusively as an illegal underground military wing
qs.e: Cadre parties rely on a select group of prominent individuals, political elites, and financiers, focusing on leadership quality rather than building massive, broad-based membership lists.

qs.q: Pressure groups organized specifically to promote cause-oriented goals (such as human rights or environmental protection) are classified as
qs.e: Cause or attitudinal interest groups are formed by people seeking to promote specific moral, environmental, or social causes (e.g. Amnesty International, environmental groups), rather than commercial self-interest.

qs.q: Within civil service organizational hierarchy, top policy-formulating officials belong to the
qs.e: The Administrative Class is the highest cadre of the civil service, responsible for policy formulation, advising ministers, and overall departmental management.

qs.q: Nigeria's foreign policy toward immediate neighboring countries in West Africa is guided primarily by the principle of
o: Ideological confrontation and export of revolution
qs.e: Good neighborliness promotes peaceful coexistence, non-aggression, border cooperation, and mutual assistance between Nigeria and its immediate neighbors (Benin, Niger, Chad, Cameroon).

qs.q: Under past military regimes in Nigeria, the supreme legislative and executive ruling council was the
o: Supreme Military Council (SMC) / Armed Forces Ruling Council (AFRC)
qs.e: Military regimes concentrated legislative and executive power in a supreme ruling body—variously named the Supreme Military Council (SMC), Armed Forces Ruling Council (AFRC), or Provisional Ruling Council (PRC).

qs.q: A legal sovereign possesses de jure authority to enact laws, but if it cannot enforce those laws due to widespread rebellion, it lacks
o: De facto power and effective administrative control
qs.e: De jure authority means lawful right under the constitution. De facto power means actual physical and administrative control. A government losing physical control lacks de facto power.

qs.q: A key distinction between a pure market economy (Capitalism) and a Mixed Economy is that a Mixed Economy
o: Combines private enterprise with strategic state intervention and welfare provision
Abolishes all forms of private commerce and individual land rights
Prohibits government agencies from collecting taxes or building infrastructure
Operates entirely without paper currency or commercial banking
qs.e: A mixed economy incorporates both private business ownership and state regulation/public enterprise to balance economic efficiency with social welfare goals.

qs.q: In a unitary system of government, power is concentrated at the central level, meaning sub-national divisions exercise authority that is
o: Delegated to them by the central government and revocable by central statute
Guaranteed as constitutionally sovereign and permanent
Superior to central government executive orders
qs.e: In a unitary state (like the UK or Ghana), central authority holds supreme power. Powers granted to regional or local councils are delegated by the central parliament and can be altered or abolished by ordinary legislation.

qs.q: How can administrative tribunals pose a potential risk to A.V. Dicey's concept of the Rule of Law?
o: They may operate outside standard judicial procedure and consist of executive appointees rather than independent judges
They enforce criminal convictions without allowing police participation
They automatically strike down acts of parliament without legislative review
They operate exclusively in foreign diplomatic missions
qs.e: Administrative tribunals are executive-led bodies handling specialized disputes. Dicey warned that using administrative tribunals instead of ordinary courts of law could undermine strict legal equality and judicial independence.

qs.q: Under the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, the impeachment of the President or Vice-President requires a multi-step process culminating in a vote of
o: Not less than two-thirds majority of all members of each House of the National Assembly
Simple majority of the Senate and unanimous consent of state governors
Three-fourths majority of the Supreme Court panel of justices
Unanimous address issued by the National Judicial Council
qs.e: Section 143 of the 1999 Constitution lays out impeachment: a notice of allegation, investigation by a 7-person panel appointed by the CJN, and if proven, adoption by a two-thirds majority vote of all members of each house of the National Assembly.

qs.q: A major argument supporting a bicameral legislature over a unicameral legislature is that bicameralism
o: Provides double scrutiny of bills and prevents hasty or ill-considered legislation
Reduces government administrative expenses and legislative delays
Eliminates deadlocks between executive ministers and senators
Concentrates lawmaking authority in a single chamber
qs.e: Bicameralism ensures that proposed laws are thoroughly scrutinized by two separate chambers, reducing errors, emotional lawmaking, and autocratic dominance by a single house.

qs.q: Section 162 of the 1999 Constitution mandates that all revenues collected by the Government of the Federation (with few exceptions) be paid into the
qs.e: Under Section 162(1) of the 1999 Constitution, the Federation Account is the special account into which all revenues collected by the Federal Government are paid, for distribution among federal, state, and local tiers.

qs.q: The 1963 Republican Constitution transformed Nigeria's legal structure by
o: Replacing the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London with the Nigerian Supreme Court as the final court of appeal
Re-establishing colonial governorships across the northern provinces
Abolishing regional legislative houses in Enugu and Ibadan
Adopting French as an official language of the federation
qs.e: The 1963 Republican Constitution severed formal ties with the British Crown, replacing the Queen with a Ceremonial President and making the Supreme Court of Nigeria the final court of appeal, ending appeals to the UK Privy Council.

qs.q: When trade unions like the Nigerian Labour Congress (NLC) declare a nationwide general strike, they are employing
o: Direct action to pressure government into policy concessions
Judicial litigation before the International Court of Justice
Lobbying through private parliamentary dinner receptions
qs.e: General strikes, picketing, and boycotts are forms of direct action utilized by labor unions to exert economic and public pressure on government authorities during disputes.

qs.q: In electoral systems, single-member constituencies operate on the principle that
o: Each electoral district elects exactly one candidate to represent it in the legislature
Multiple political parties share five legislative seats per district
Voters choose ten representatives per district from a single party list
Districts are abolished in favor of a single national voting unit
qs.e: Single-member districts (constituencies) elect one representative each (as in Nigeria's House of Representatives elections), contrasting with multi-member proportional representation districts.

qs.q: Bureaucratic red tape in public administration refers to
o: Excessive adherence to rigid rules, formal procedure, and paperwork that delays service delivery
The physical boundaries marking administrative buildings
Confidential security classifications placed on cabinet budget files
The political alignment of civil servants with ruling parties
qs.e: 'Red tape' describes cumbersome official routines, superfluous paperwork, and strict rule enforcement that slow down decision-making and public service delivery.

qs.q: The 1976 Local Government Reforms in Nigeria sought to secure local government financial stability by mandating
o: Direct statutory allocations from both the Federal Account and State Government revenues
The total privatization of local market revenues to foreign investors
The abolition of state government tax collection powers
Direct loans from international commercial banks without central bank approval
qs.e: The 1976 reforms entitled local governments to statutory allocations paid directly from the federal revenue account and a percentage of state internally generated revenues.

qs.q: Under Nigerian law, a Nigerian citizen by birth who voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another country (other than by marriage) may face
o: Loss of Nigerian citizenship if they were not born in Nigeria, subject to dual citizenship constitutional exceptions
Automatic imprisonment without trial by magistrate courts
Confiscation of all personal inherited landed properties
Permanent prohibition from entering any commercial bank
qs.e: Section 28 of the 1999 Constitution specifies dual citizenship rules: a citizen by birth retains Nigerian citizenship even if acquiring another citizenship, whereas citizens by registration/naturalization forfeit Nigerian citizenship if they acquire another nationality.

qs.q: The Technical Aid Corps (TAC) scheme was instituted by Nigeria in 1987 to
o: Deploy Nigerian professionals to assist developing nations in Africa, the Caribbean, and Pacific regions
Recruit foreign military advisers for West African anti-insurgency operations
Export crude oil at discounted prices to European trading partners
Fund infrastructure development in local government councils across Nigeria
qs.e: The TAC scheme was established under President Babangida as a foreign policy tool to project Nigerian soft power by sending qualified volunteers (teachers, doctors, engineers) to needy ACP countries.

qs.q: Elite Theory in political sociology, as expounded by theorists like Vilfredo Pareto and C. Wright Mills, posits that in all societies
o: A small, cohesive minority holding key institutional positions makes major political decisions, regardless of democratic forms
Power is equally distributed among competing interest groups and trade unions
The majority working class exercises direct sovereign control through referendums
Political authority is rotated randomly among ordinary citizens every year
qs.e: Elite theory argues that a small economic, political, and military elite holds real power in society, shaping policy outcomes while democratic elections serve largely as formal legitimacy mechanisms.

qs.q: In common law constitutional systems, the legal doctrine of stare decisis mandates that courts must
o: Follow established legal precedents set by higher courts in similar previous cases
Nullify statutory acts passed by parliament without judicial hearings
Consult international treaties before deciding local property disputes
Refer all constitutional disputes directly to executive ministers for arbitration
qs.e: Stare decisis ('to stand by things decided') requires lower courts to follow binding legal precedents set by superior courts, maintaining consistency and predictability in judicial interpretation.

qs.q: The doctrine of Ultra Vires applies to administrative delegated legislation when an administrative regulation
o: Exceeds the statutory scope or power conferred by the parent enabling Act of parliament
Is enacted directly by a two-thirds vote of the National Assembly
Is approved unanimously by the cabinet of ministers
Is published in the official government gazette before implementation
qs.e: Ultra Vires ('beyond powers') means an administrative body or minister acted outside the authority granted by the enabling legislation. Courts invalidate such regulations as unlawful.

qs.q: Fiscal centralism in Nigeria's federal system has been criticized primarily because it
o: Concentrates main revenue collection (petroleum, customs) with the central government, leaving states financially dependent on federal allocations
Grants state governments exclusive authority to issue national currency and levy import tariffs
Abolishes statutory revenue sharing between central and state governments
Forces local government councils to fund federal defense expenditures
qs.e: Fiscal centralism centralizes oil and tax revenues in the Federation Account, creating financial dependency where state governments rely heavily on monthly federal distributions rather than generating independent revenue.

qs.q: The controversial 1979 Supreme Court ruling in Awolowo v. Shagari centered on the legal interpretation of what constitutional requirement?
o: What constituted two-thirds of 19 states in the presidential election criteria
Whether the military head of state possessed power to veto judicial decisions
The legality of state governors forming political party coalitions
The definition of universal adult suffrage in northern voting districts
qs.e: The 1979 presidential election required winning 25% of votes in two-thirds of 19 states. The court held that two-thirds of 19 states was 12 2/3 states (rather than 13 states), declaring Shehu Shagari elected.

qs.q: The political party spectrum of Nigeria's Second Republic (1979-1983) mirrored the First Republic primarily because
o: The major parties (NPN, UPN, NPP) drew their principal support from the same regional and ethnic bases as NPC, AG, and NCNC
All political parties were forced to merge into a single national vanguard party
Political parties were prohibited from campaigning outside their state capitals
Parties were funded entirely by foreign international organizations
qs.e: Despite constitutional Federal Character rules, NPN inherited the NPC's northern base, UPN inherited AG's Yoruba base, and NPP inherited NCNC's Igbo base, reflecting First Republic regional political alignments.

qs.q: The Allison Ayida Panel of 1994 recommended reversing key elements of the 1988 Civil Service Reform by
o: Restoring the title and role of Permanent Secretary as career accounting officer of ministries
Politicizing all civil service cadres down to clerical levels
Abolishing civil service pensions and tenure protections
Transferring civil service oversight to state high court judges
qs.e: The Ayida Panel reviewed the 1988 Dotun Philips reforms, restoring the post of Permanent Secretary as career non-partisan accounting officer and reducing political patronage in administration.

qs.q: The practice of state governors appointing Caretaker Committees to run local government councils in Nigeria is widely viewed as unconstitutional because
o: Section 7 of the 1999 Constitution guarantees a system of democratically elected local government councils
Caretaker committees are appointed by the Federal National Assembly rather than state assemblies
Local government chairmen must be appointed by traditional emirs and obas
Caretaker committees are legally restricted to managing state police forces
qs.e: Section 7(1) of the 1999 Constitution guarantees democratically elected local government councils. Supreme Court judgments have repeatedly declared appointed caretaker committees illegal.

qs.q: In 1997, ECOMOG forces under Nigerian military leadership intervened in Sierra Leone primarily to
o: Reinstate the democratically elected government of President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah following a military junta coup
Annex the diamond mines of Freetown into the Nigerian federation
Block UN peacekeepers from entering West Africa
Enforce maritime customs tariffs along the Atlantic coast
qs.e: ECOMOG troops deployed to Sierra Leone to reverse the 1997 military coup by the AFRC/RUF junta and restore the democratically elected civilian government of President Tejan Kabbah.

qs.q: The 1963 compromise in Addis Ababa that led to the founding of the OAU reconciled which two opposing diplomatic blocs of African states?
o: The conservative Monrovia Group and the radical Casablanca Group
The Commonwealth Group and the Francophone Union
The Non-Aligned Movement and the Warsaw Pact
The ECOWAS Alliance and the Maghreb League
qs.e: The OAU was formed as a compromise between the Casablanca Group (advocating immediate political union under Nkrumah) and the Monrovia Group (advocating gradual economic cooperation and sovereignty respect led by Balewa/Tubman).

qs.q: A key factor that precipitated the July 1975 military coup against General Yakubu Gowon was his
o: Indefinite postponement of the promised transition date to civilian democratic rule
Attempt to abolish the Nigerian Armed Forces and police
Decision to sign a military defense pact with South Africa
Immediate creation of 50 new states across the federation
qs.e: Gowon had pledged to return Nigeria to civilian rule in 1976, but in October 1974 he declared 1976 unrealistic, causing widespread dissatisfaction within the military and public, leading to Murtala Muhammed's coup in July 1975.

qs.q: In political philosophy, Hannah Arendt differentiated Totalitarianism from traditional Authoritarianism by emphasizing that Totalitarianism seeks to
o: Reshape human nature and control every aspect of private and public life through ideological terror and total mobilization
Maintain traditional social hierarchies while ignoring the private lives of citizens
Limit state power strictly to external defense and tax collection
Establish multi-party democratic governance through local council elections
qs.e: Arendt argued that while authoritarian regimes demand political obedience and leave private sphere intact, totalitarian regimes use terror and ideology to eliminate civil society and exert total control over individuals.

qs.q: The 1989 Constitution designed under General Ibrahim Babangida was structurally unique because it mandated a
o: Grassroots two-party system (SDP and NRC) created and funded by the federal military government
Multi-party system with unlimited registration of political associations
Permanent single-party socialist framework led by military officers
Hereditary monarchy with a ceremonial prime minister
qs.e: The 1989 Third Republic Constitution introduced a state-constructed two-party system—the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and National Republican Convention (NRC)—designed by the Babangida military regime.

qs.q: The Concert of Medium Powers (also known as the Lagos Forum), initiated by Nigeria in 1987, was designed to
o: Create an influential diplomatic bridge between super-power military blocs and enhance South-South cooperation
Form an exclusive economic alliance of OPEC oil-exporting states
Establish a West African military defense force to fight piracy
Enforce strict tariff protectionism across developing economies
qs.e: Initiated by Foreign Minister Bolaji Akinyemi in 1987, the Lagos Forum brought together leading middle-power nations (such as Nigeria, Brazil, India, Egypt, Mexico) to act as an impartial coalition in global diplomacy.

qs.q: The Structural Adjustment Programs (SAP) imposed on African nations by the IMF and World Bank during the 1880s-1990s impacted state sovereignty by
o: Constraining national policy-making through mandatory conditionalities like currency devaluation, deregulation, and public sector retrenchment
Forcing developing nations to surrender foreign diplomatic representation to the UN Secretariat
Abolishing national legislative assemblies and replacing them with IMF boards
Requiring developing states to adopt the US dollar as sole legal tender
qs.e: SAP conditionalities mandated structural economic reforms (privatization, trade liberalization, subsidy removal, currency devaluation), effectively transferring key sovereign economic decisions from domestic parliaments to external international financial institutions.

qs.q: In electoral redistricting, Gerrymandering through the technique of 'packing' involves
o: Concentrating opposition voters into a few electoral districts to minimize their overall influence across remaining districts
Spreading opposition voters thinly across many districts so they never achieve a majority
Randomly assigning voters to constituencies regardless of geographic location
Abolishing electoral constituency borders prior to voting
qs.e: 'Packing' concentrates as many voters of an opposing party into one district as possible, conceding that single district but diluting their voting strength in surrounding districts ('cracking').

qs.q: In a parliamentary system of government, the executive power is held by the Prime Minister who is chosen from
o: The majority party or coalition in parliament
The highest bench of the judicial council
The supreme traditional council of chiefs
qs.e: In a parliamentary system, the Prime Minister is the leader of the majority party (or coalition) in parliament and is drawn directly from the legislative body.

qs.q: The primary objective of establishing local government administration is to
o: Bring governance closer to grassroots citizens and deliver local public services
Manage foreign diplomatic embassies in overseas territories
Enact federal criminal statutes and issue national currency
Command regional military garrisons during national emergencies
qs.e: Local government exists as the third tier of government to facilitate grassroots political participation, address local needs, and deliver basic infrastructure and services.

qs.q: A political regime that exercises complete, unrestricted control over both public policy and the private lives of its citizens is described as
qs.e: Totalitarianism is an extreme form of authoritarianism where the state seeks total control over all public and private aspects of society, suppressing all civil liberties.

qs.q: Fundamental human rights are embedded in a democratic constitution primarily to
o: Protect individual citizens from arbitrary state power and oppression
Enable executive governors to bypass legislative court orders
Grant political parties exemption from national election laws
Allow public servants to set their own salaries without oversight
qs.e: Entrenching fundamental rights in a constitution guarantees individual liberties (life, speech, movement) against state encroachment and arbitrary executive power.

qs.q: The international law principle of non-interference prohibits sovereign states from
o: Intervening in the internal domestic affairs of another sovereign nation
Joining multilateral trade bodies like the World Trade Organization
Signing bilateral cultural exchange agreements with foreign allies
Participating in UN General Assembly annual debates
qs.e: Non-interference (Article 2 of UN Charter) mandates that states must refrain from meddling in the internal sovereign matters and domestic jurisdiction of other independent nations.

qs.q: Trade unions primarily represent the interests of
o: Workers and employees in specific industries or professions
Foreign diplomatic envoys residing in capital cities
qs.e: Trade unions (like the NLC or TUC) are organized associations of workers created to protect and promote their economic rights, working conditions, and wages through collective bargaining.

qs.q: A one-party system is a political setup where
o: Only one single political party is constitutionally recognized to form the government
All political parties are banned from operating in national elections
Two major political parties share executive cabinet appointments
Regional political parties control every local council
qs.e: In a one-party state, only one political party has the legal right to form the government, and opposition parties are outlawed or restricted.

qs.q: How does parliament exercise legislative oversight over executive ministries?
o: Through standing committees investigating executive spending, policy implementation, and administrative conduct
By issuing direct judicial arrest warrants against cabinet ministers
By appointing regional military commanders to head civil ministries
By dissolving state houses of assembly across the federation
qs.e: Legislative oversight is performed by parliamentary committees that review executive department budgets, conduct investigative hearings, and monitor administration of laws.

qs.q: A key formal characteristic of a written constitution is that it
o: Is embodied in a single legal document enacted at a specific historical moment
Consists entirely of unwritten traditional customs and royal proclamations
Can be altered at any time by a simple verbal decree of the President
Excludes judicial interpretation by constitutional high courts
qs.e: A written (codified) constitution is contained in a single organic document that sets out the framework of governance, rights, and distribution of powers.

qs.q: The power of judicial review allows the judiciary to invalidate legislative enactments that
o: Violate constitutional provisions or exceed statutory powers
Increase annual budget allocations for education and health
Are passed by a unanimous vote in the Senate
Are supported by popular national petitions
qs.e: Judicial review empowers courts to declare laws or executive actions null and void if they contradict express provisions or principles of the supreme constitution.

qs.q: In Nigeria's federal structure, matters on the Residual Legislative List fall under the exclusive lawmaking power of
qs.e: The Residual List comprises all subjects not listed on either the Exclusive or Concurrent lists; these residual matters belong exclusively to state legislatures.

qs.q: Nigeria adopted an Executive Presidential system of government for the first time under the
qs.e: The 1979 Constitution introduced an executive presidential system modeled after the United States, replacing the British-style parliamentary system used in the First Republic.

qs.q: In the 1964 Nigerian Federal Elections, the two major political alliances that contested power were the
o: United Progressive Grand Alliance (UPGA) and Nigerian National Alliance (NNA)
Action Group (AG) and Northern People's Congress (NPC)
National Party of Nigeria (NPN) and Unity Party of Nigeria (UPN)
Social Democratic Party (SDP) and National Republican Convention (NRC)
qs.e: The 1964 elections saw the formation of two broad alliances: UPGA (NCNC, AG, UMBC, NEPU) and NNA (NPC, NNDP led by Akintola).

qs.q: The Civil Service Commission is constitutionally empowered to
o: Recruit, appoint, promote, and discipline civil servants
Enact statutory legislation for public corporations
Audit central bank monetary policy decisions
Appoint judges to state high courts
qs.e: The Civil Service Commission is an independent executive body responsible for managing civil service human resources—recruitment, promotions, transfers, and disciplinary actions.

qs.q: The civil service convention of anonymity means that
o: Civil servants work behind the scenes and the political minister takes public responsibility for departmental decisions
Civil servants must wear masks when appearing before legislative committees
The names of public servants cannot be published in official government payrolls
Civil servants are prohibited from signing official administrative letters
qs.e: Anonymity shields civil servants from public praise or blame; the politically responsible Minister takes public credit or criticism for policies executed by civil servants.

qs.q: In an Absolute Majority electoral system, a candidate is declared elected only if they obtain
o: More than 50 percent of the total valid votes cast
The highest votes cast even if under 30 percent
Two-thirds of all votes in rural constituencies
A unanimous vote from all polling agents
qs.e: An absolute majority requires a winning candidate to secure more than half of the total votes cast (50% + 1 vote).

qs.q: Under the 1999 Constitution, a foreign woman married to a Nigerian citizen may acquire Nigerian citizenship through
qs.e: Section 26 of the 1999 Constitution allows a foreign woman married to a Nigerian citizen to acquire Nigerian citizenship by registration upon fulfilling statutory conditions.

qs.q: A major internal factor that historically invited military intervention in West African politics was
o: Widespread corruption, election rigging, and political instability among civilian elites
Excessive economic surpluses accumulated by state local councils
Over-compliance with constitutional court orders by ruling parties
The complete absence of political parties during civilian regimes
qs.e: Military interventions in post-colonial West Africa were frequently triggered by governance failures: political corruption, electoral malpractice, ethnic polarization, and civil disorder.

qs.q: In Almond and Verba's typology of political culture, a 'Subject Political Culture' is one where citizens are
o: Aware of central government outputs and laws but passive regarding political participation and input
Completely unaware of national government institutions and politics
Highly active participants who shape policy through regular political activity
Exclusively loyal to foreign international organizations
qs.e: In a Subject political culture, citizens are aware of executive authority and laws (outputs) but see themselves as passive subjects with little ability or inclination to influence political processes (inputs).

qs.q: How does Democratic Socialism differ from a Mixed Economy in political focus?
o: Democratic Socialism prioritizes extensive social equality and public welfare through democratic planning, whereas a Mixed Economy focuses on balancing private capital with state regulation
Democratic Socialism outlaws all private trade unions, while a Mixed Economy mandates them
Democratic Socialism operates under single-party rule, while a Mixed Economy has no constitution
Democratic Socialism abolishes national parliaments in favor of corporate boards
qs.e: Democratic Socialism emphasizes transforming capitalist structures democratically to achieve social equality and public ownership of key assets, whereas a Mixed Economy retains capitalism while introducing state regulatory balance.

qs.q: An executive usurpation of legislative authority occurs when the President
o: Issues executive orders that alter or enact laws without parliamentary statutory authorization
Vetoes a legislative bill returned by parliament
Submits annual budget estimates to the National Assembly
Pardons convicted criminals under prerogative powers
qs.e: Executive usurpation occurs when the executive branch exceeds its constitutional mandate by enacting substantive laws via decrees or administrative orders without legislative authorization.

qs.q: In parliamentary assemblies, Standing Committees differ from Select Committees because Standing Committees are
o: Permanent committees established to process bills within specific policy areas throughout the legislative session
Temporary committees set up to investigate a specific ad-hoc issue and disband afterward
Joint committees comprising judges and cabinet ministers
Secret committees appointed exclusively by traditional rulers
qs.e: Standing Committees are permanent bodies created by legislative rules to handle bills in specific domains (e.g., finance, defense). Select Committees are temporary bodies created for specific investigations.

qs.q: In legal systems based on Civil Law codes (like France), judicial precedents are generally
o: Less binding than codified statutory laws, as judges apply statutory codes rather than past rulings
Strictly binding on all superior and lower courts above statutory codes
Prohibited from being cited by defense legal practitioners
Formulated exclusively by military ruling councils
qs.e: Civil Law systems rely primarily on comprehensive written codes enacted by legislatures. Court precedents are persuasive rather than strictly binding, contrasting with Common Law systems where precedents form core law.

qs.q: The National Economic Council (NEC) in Nigeria serves as an intergovernmental relations body comprising the
o: Vice-President as Chairman, State Governors, and the Central Bank Governor
President, Speaker of the House, and Chief Justice
All 774 Local Government Chairmen and traditional emirs
Foreign diplomatic ambassadors and ECOWAS commissioners
qs.e: Under the 1999 Constitution (Third Schedule), the NEC is chaired by the Vice-President and includes all 36 State Governors and the Central Bank Governor to advise on economic coordination.

qs.q: The main purpose of Section 308 (Immunity Clause) in the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria is to protect incumbent executives from
o: Distractions caused by civil or criminal legal proceedings while performing official duties
Impeachment proceedings initiated by two-thirds of the National Assembly
Losing political party primaries during national re-elections
Being audited by the Auditor-General of the Federation
qs.e: Section 308 protects the President, Vice-President, Governors, and Deputy Governors from legal proceedings while in office, ensuring they can discharge executive duties without court harassment.

qs.q: The Action Group (AG) party in Nigeria's First Republic gained widespread popular support in the Western Region primarily through its policy of
o: Free primary education, free healthcare, and regional agricultural development
Immediate nationalization of all foreign commercial banks
Abolishing regional legislative assemblies across Nigeria
Establishing a single-party socialist political state
qs.e: The AG, led by Chief Obafemi Awolowo, implemented popular social-democratic programs in the Western Region, notably the pioneering Free Primary Education scheme introduced in 1955.

qs.q: Insider pressure groups differ from outsider pressure groups because insider groups
o: Enjoy regular, direct access to government ministers and decision-makers for policy consultations
Rely exclusively on illegal street protests, riots, and violent blockades
Operate outside the country without formal registration
Are banned from submitting policy briefs to legislative committees
qs.e: Insider groups have established consultative status and work closely with government officials/ministries. Outsider groups lack direct access and rely on public campaigning and protests.

qs.q: The electoral practice of artificially altering constituency boundaries to give an unfair advantage to a particular political party is known as
qs.e: Gerrymandering is the manipulation of electoral district boundaries to favor one political party or demographic group over others.

qs.q: In administrative decentralization, Devolution differs from Deconcentration because Devolution involves
o: Transferring political, legal, and financial authority to autonomous local government units
Shifting administrative tasks to field offices while retaining central control
Selling state-owned enterprises to private corporate investors
Merging regional ministries into a central national bureau
qs.e: Devolution transfers political power and decision-making authority to autonomous sub-national bodies. Deconcentration merely decentralizes administrative workload to field staff without transferring political power.

qs.q: The General Orders (now Public Service Rules) in the civil service serve as
o: A comprehensive body of administrative rules governing civil servants' conduct, duties, and conditions of service
Constitutional statutes passed by parliament to appoint court judges
Military decrees regulating emergency defense operations
International trade treaties governing port tariffs
qs.e: Public Service Rules (formerly General Orders) are administrative regulations specifying the terms of employment, rights, duties, discipline, and operational procedures for civil servants.

qs.q: During the anti-apartheid struggle, Nigeria earned recognition as a 'Frontline State' despite its geographical location in West Africa because of its
o: Extensive financial, diplomatic, and material support for liberation movements in Southern Africa
Direct military invasion of South African coastal cities
Deployment of peacekeepers under British colonial command
Creation of a southern African free trade customs union
qs.e: Nigeria was declared an honorary Frontline State by Southern African nations due to its heavy financial contributions, diplomatic leadership, and sponsorship of anti-apartheid movements (ANC, PAC, SWAPO, ZANU).

qs.q: In the United Nations General Assembly, decision-making on ordinary questions operates on the principle of
o: Simple majority vote where each member state possesses one vote
Veto power exercised exclusively by five permanent member nations
Weighted voting based on national economic GDP contributions
Unanimous consent of all 193 member states
qs.e: The UN General Assembly operates on sovereign equality: each state has one vote. Decisions on ordinary matters require a simple majority; important questions require a two-thirds majority.

qs.q: A democratic regime faces a Crisis of Legitimacy when
o: A substantial portion of citizens no longer accepts the moral right or authority of government to rule
The legislature passes a balanced annual budget on schedule
The Supreme Court upholds a constitutional amendment unanimously
The military command council pledges allegiance to the civilian president
qs.e: A legitimacy crisis occurs when government authority breaks down because citizens view institutional processes or political leaders as invalid, corrupt, or unrepresentative.

qs.q: During a State of Emergency declared under Section 305 of the 1999 Constitution, executive powers are expanded, raising legal concerns because emergency regulations may
o: Temporarily restrict certain fundamental human rights and expand executive detention powers
Permanently abolish the Supreme Court of Nigeria
Transfer all national revenue to state local government chairmen
Mandate immediate parliamentary elections every month
qs.e: States of emergency grant extraordinary powers to the executive to restore order, but risk infringing upon fundamental civil liberties like freedom of movement, assembly, and personal liberty.

qs.q: The constitutional requirement that any amendment altering the creation of new states in Nigeria requires approval by two-thirds of the National Assembly and 24 State Assemblies demonstrates that Nigeria's constitution is
o: Rigid, ensuring sub-national units must consent to major structural alterations
Flexible, allowing rapid legislative changes during emergency sessions
Unwritten, relying on parliamentary conventions rather than clauses
Unitary, concentrating all amendment power in the central executive
qs.e: The high hurdle for constitutional amendments—requiring two-thirds of National Assembly members and resolutions by at least 24 of the 36 State Houses of Assembly—exemplifies a rigid federal constitution.

qs.q: The 1964/65 constitutional standoff between President Nnamdi Azikiwe and Prime Minister Abubakar Tafawa Balewa arose because Azikiwe initially refused to
o: Invite Balewa to form a new government following widespread boycott and allegations of rigging in the 1964 elections
Sign the national defense budget passed by the House of Representatives
Appoint Supreme Court justices recommended by the regional judiciaries
Relocate the federal capital from Lagos to Kaduna
qs.e: Following the heavily boycotted and disputed 1964 federal elections, President Azikiwe refused to reappoint Balewa as Prime Minister, creating a tense constitutional deadlock resolved only after inter-party negotiations.

qs.q: The Northern Elements Progressive Union (NEPU), led by Mallam Aminu Kano during the First Republic, positioned itself politically as the defender of the
o: Talakawa (peasantry/commoners) against traditional feudal oppression and conservative elites
Royal emirate aristocracies and hereditary native authorities
Southern cocoa merchants expanding commercial cartels
Foreign colonial trading companies operating in the North
qs.e: NEPU was a populist democratic party in northern Nigeria that challenged the traditional feudal power of the Native Authorities and NPC, fighting for the political and social rights of the Talakawa (commoners).

qs.q: The January 2012 nationwide strikes organized by the NLC and TUC demonstrated pressure group power by compelling the Federal Government to
o: Partial reduction of deregulated petrol prices following mass public protests
Dissolve the National Assembly and call immediate fresh elections
Abolish the Federal Ministry of Petroleum Resources
Privatize all state high courts across Nigeria
qs.e: The 'Occupy Nigeria' general strike organized by labor unions in January 2012 shut down economic activities across the nation, forcing the federal government to reduce the price of PMS (fuel).

qs.q: In public financial administration, Performance-Based Budgeting differs from Line-Item Budgeting because Performance-Based Budgeting allocates funds based on
o: Measurable outputs, program outcomes, and objectives achieved rather than historical expenditure heads
Strict historical departmental spending patterns without evaluation
The political party seniority of ministry accounting officers
Arbitrary monthly central bank cash draws
qs.e: Performance-based budgeting links funding directly to measurable results and specific policy goals, whereas traditional line-item budgeting focuses simply on listing inputs and historical spending heads.

qs.q: Nigeria's diplomatic handling of the Bakassi Peninsula judgment by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in 2002 demonstrated commitment to
o: Peaceful settlement of international disputes through adherence to international law treaties
Unilateral military re-invasion and rejection of international tribunal rulings
Immediate withdrawal from the United Nations General Assembly
Forming a bilateral military alliance against Cameroon
qs.e: Despite domestic political opposition, Nigeria respected the 2002 ICJ ruling and negotiated the Green Tree Agreement (2006) for a peaceful transfer of Bakassi, reinforcing its commitment to international law.

qs.q: Nigeria's membership in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) influences its domestic budget planning because OPEC
o: Sets crude oil production quotas that limit Nigeria's petroleum export volumes and revenue forecasts
Fixes domestic tax rates on agricultural exports in member states
Mandates the privatized sale of state refineries to foreign banks
Requires member countries to abolish national currencies
qs.e: As an OPEC member (joined 1971), Nigeria must comply with assigned oil production quotas, which directly affect national crude oil output levels and federal budget revenue projections.

qs.q: The December 31, 1983 military coup led by Major-General Muhammadu Buhari ousted the Second Republic civilian government primarily due to
o: Rampant economic mismanagement, severe corruption, and widespread rigging in the 1983 elections
The civilian government's decision to ban the armed forces
The signing of a military defense pact with foreign socialist states
The creation of 100 new local government councils
qs.e: The 1983 coup ended Shehu Shagari's civilian government following severe economic crisis, inflation, systemic corruption, and electoral malpractices surrounding the 1983 general elections.

qs.q: During the military administration of General Sani Abacha (1993-1998), Nigeria suffered international diplomatic isolation and suspension from the Commonwealth following the
o: Execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other Ogoni civil rights activists in 1995
Nationalization of foreign oil multinational corporate assets
Deployment of ECOMOG peacekeepers to Sierra Leone
Boycott of the 1996 Olympic Games in Atlanta
qs.e: The execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight fellow Ogoni leaders in November 1995 provoked international outrage, leading to Nigeria's immediate suspension from the Commonwealth of Nations and global sanctions.

qs.q: In political theory, Anarchism rejects state authority fundamentally because it asserts that
o: The state is inherently oppressive and unnecessary, advocating voluntary self-governing cooperative associations instead
The state should be expanded to own all land and corporate capital
Society can only function under absolute hereditary monarchies
Laws should be codified exclusively by international religious councils
qs.e: Anarchism posits that compulsory state government is undesirable and harmful, proposing that human society can organize itself voluntarily without hierarchical political authority or state coercion.

qs.q: The fierce religious controversy over the proposed Federal Sharia Court of Appeal that threatened to derail the 1979 Constitution occurred during which historic body’s proceedings?
o: Federal Sharia Court of Appeal, which divided delegates along religious and regional lines
Unicameral National Assembly replacing the Senate
Permanent Military Advisory Council in the presidency
Single national police force managed by state governors
qs.e: The proposal to establish a Federal Sharia Court of Appeal triggered intense debate in the 1977-78 Constituent Assembly, threatening to derail the constitution until a compromise was brokered limiting Sharia courts to state levels.

qs.q: A recurring dilemma in Nigeria's foreign policy implementation is balancing its Afrocentric diplomatic commitments with its
o: Domestic economic challenges, national security imperatives, and sovereign self-interest
Mandatory obligations under the Warsaw Pact defense treaty
Constitutional requirement to annex neighboring territories
Commitment to enforcing a single West African state religion
qs.e: Foreign policy analysts note that Nigeria's generous Afrocentric posture (peacekeeping, aid, liberation support) often strains domestic economic resources, creating tension between regional leadership and internal national development needs.

qs.q: African nations advocating UN Security Council reform under the Ezulwini Consensus demand
o: At least two permanent seats with veto power and five non-permanent seats for Africa on the Security Council
The complete abolition of the UN Security Council and General Assembly
Transferring UN headquarters from New York to Geneva permanently
Restricting Security Council permanent membership exclusively to European nations
qs.e: Adopted by the AU in 2005 in Ezulwini, Eswatini, the Ezulwini Consensus outlines Africa's common position: demanding at least two permanent seats with full veto rights and five non-permanent seats on the UN Security Council.

qs.q: In preferential voting systems, the Alternative Vote (AV) mechanism ensures a candidate is elected by requiring voters to
o: Rank candidates preferentially, redistributing lowest candidates' second-choice votes until one candidate achieves over 50 percent
Cast a single vote for a political party list without choosing candidates
Select two candidates from opposing parties on a combined ballot
Submit written essays explaining their political choices
qs.e: Under the Alternative Vote (Instant-Runoff Voting), voters rank candidates (1, 2, 3...). If no candidate wins an absolute majority of first-preference votes, the lowest candidate is eliminated and their votes redistributed to voters' second choices until a majority is achieved.

qs.q: The main distinction between a pressure group and a political party regarding membership focus is that pressure groups generally
o: Represent narrow, specific sectional or professional interests, whereas political parties seek broad appeal to win elections
Restrict membership exclusively to elected members of parliament
Mandate that all members hold public administrative offices
Prohibit members from participating in civil society protests
qs.e: Pressure groups focus on specific interest areas (e.g. medical practitioners, oil workers, environmentalists) to promote narrow goals, while political parties formulate broad platforms to attract diverse electorates and gain political power.

qs.q: Which of the following represents a constitutionally recognized mode of acquiring citizenship in Nigeria?
o: Military service, Parliamentary vote, and University graduation
Diplomatic appointment, Judicial ruling, and Chieftaincy conferment
qs.e: Under Chapter III of the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, citizenship can be acquired through three modes: by birth (Section 25), by registration (Section 26), or by naturalization (Section 27).

qs.q: The primary function of the judicial arm of government is to
o: Interpret laws and adjudicate disputes between individuals, entities, and government
Enact statutory legislation and annual budget laws
Enforce police regulations and military orders
qs.e: The constitutional role of the judiciary is to interpret statutes, apply the constitution, and resolve disputes between citizens or between citizens and the state.

qs.q: A fundamental feature of a capitalist economic system is
o: Private ownership of property and the means of production
State ownership of all industrial factories and land
Centralized economic planning by government ministries
The total prohibition of private corporate profits
qs.e: Capitalism is characterized by private ownership of assets, capital accumulation, competitive markets, and profit-driven enterprise.

qs.q: Local government councils in Nigeria receive statutory financial allocations directly from the
qs.e: Under Section 162 of the 1999 Constitution, local government councils are entitled to statutory allocations distributed from the Federation Account.

qs.q: The overriding objective of any nation's foreign policy is to protect and promote its
qs.e: National interest—encompassing territorial integrity, national security, economic prosperity, and sovereign independence—is the fundamental driving goal of foreign policy.

qs.q: The international headquarters of the United Nations Organization (UNO) is located in
qs.e: The official headquarters of the United Nations is in New York City, USA, where the General Assembly and Security Council regularly convene.

qs.q: The presiding officer of the House of Representatives in Nigeria's National Assembly is the
o: Speaker of the House of Representatives
qs.e: The Speaker of the House of Representatives is elected by members of the House to preside over legislative debates and maintain order.

qs.q: In political science, Sovereignty is defined as the
o: Supreme legal authority of a state to govern its territory free from external control
Power of military commanders to suspend parliamentary elections
Right of international organizations to rewrite domestic constitutions
Capacity of trade unions to organize general nationwide strikes
qs.e: Sovereignty is the ultimate legal power and authority of a state to make and enforce laws within its defined territory without external interference.

qs.q: An example of a constitutional convention in the unwritten political system of the United Kingdom is that
o: The Monarch assents to bills passed by Parliament as a matter of obligatory custom
The Prime Minister appoints Supreme Court judges without parliamentary oversight
Parliament is dissolved automatically every twelve months
Citizens vote directly on all cabinet executive decrees
qs.e: By convention, the British Monarch always grants Royal Assent to bills passed by both Houses of Parliament, even though legally the Crown possesses formal veto rights.

qs.q: The principle of equality before the law dictates that
o: No citizen or public official is above the law, and all are subject to the jurisdiction of ordinary courts
All citizens must earn equal monthly salaries regardless of employment
Public officials cannot be prosecuted for criminal offenses during their tenure
Rich and poor citizens are tried in separate specialized court systems
qs.e: Equality before the law means all individuals—regardless of social rank, wealth, or political position—are bound by the same general laws and tried in the same ordinary courts.

qs.q: In an executive presidential system, cabinet ministers are appointed by the President and must
o: Resign their legislative seats if selected from parliament, preserving separation of powers
Remain active voting members of the House of Representatives
Serve co-currently as presiding judges in state high courts
Hold life tenure free from presidential dismissal
qs.e: Under presidential separation of powers (e.g., Section 147(4) of Nigeria's 1999 Constitution), if a member of parliament is appointed as a minister, they must vacate their legislative seat.

qs.q: Fiscal federalism refers to the system of
o: Financial and revenue allocation relationships among different tiers of government in a federation
Direct central bank control over private commercial bank interest rates
Military regulation of international import and export tariffs
Unilateral tax collection by local government traditional rulers
qs.e: Fiscal federalism deals with the allocation of taxing powers and expenditure responsibilities among federal, state, and local governments in a federal state.

qs.q: The 1954 Lyttelton Constitution introduced executive regional leadership by creating the office of
o: Premier for each of the three regions
Chief Executive Officer for local councils
qs.e: The 1954 Lyttelton Constitution created regional executive heads known as Premiers (Awolowo in West, Azikiwe in East, Ahmadu Bello in North).

qs.q: A two-party system is a political setup where
o: Two dominant political parties consistently dominate national elections and government formation
Only two political parties are legally permitted to exist by constitution
All minor parties are banned from registering candidates in local elections
The executive president and prime minister belong to opposing parties
qs.e: A two-party system is one in which two major parties dominate electoral competition and alternate holding executive power (e.g. Democrats vs Republicans in the US), even if minor parties exist.

qs.q: Pressure groups exert political influence primarily by
o: Lobbying lawmakers, mobilizing public opinion, and submitting petitions to committees
Sponsoring political party candidates in national presidential elections
Enacting statutory legislation during parliamentary sessions
Appointing judicial officers to superior courts of record
qs.e: Pressure groups attempt to influence government policy through non-electoral tactics: lobbying, public campaigns, petitions, demonstrations, and expert testimony.

qs.q: In electoral systems, a plurality system differs from a majority system because under plurality, a candidate wins by securing
o: More votes than any other single competitor, even if below an absolute majority
More than 75 percent of all registered voters in the constituency
An exact tie with the second-place candidate
A unanimous vote from the electoral commission board
qs.e: Plurality (First-Past-The-Post) requires only that a candidate get more votes than any other candidate individually. Majority requires securing more than 50% of the total vote.

qs.q: The governing board of a public corporation in Nigeria is responsible for
o: Formulating broad corporate policies, overseeing management, and ensuring operational objectives are met
Managing daily civil service personnel files in federal ministries
Passing annual statutory legislation in the House of Representatives
Presiding over criminal trials in federal high courts
qs.e: The Board of Directors of a public corporation provides strategic direction, formulates policy guidelines, and supervises management, leaving day-to-day operations to executive directors.

qs.q: In civil service administration, Meritocracy ensures that recruitment and promotion are based on
o: Qualifications, competitive examinations, competence, and performance
Political patronage and personal loyalty to ruling party leaders
Hereditary family titles and traditional chieftaincy ranks
Tribal origin and regional political quotas exclusively
qs.e: Meritocracy mandates that public servants are hired and promoted on the basis of demonstrated competence, qualifications, and merit rather than political favor or nepotism.

qs.q: In a constitutional democracy, democratic civil-military relations dictate that the military must remain
o: Subordinate to democratically elected civilian authority
Superior to the constitutional Supreme Court
Authorized to suspend parliament during economic recessions
qs.e: Democratic civilian control of the military requires that armed forces operate under the command and oversight of elected civilian officials (the President as Commander-in-Chief and Parliament).

qs.q: Political culture in a society undergoes gradual transformation over time primarily through the continuous process of
o: Political socialization across generations through institutions like families, schools, and media
Immediate military decrees issued during political crises
Unilateral judicial rulings delivered by constitutional courts
Annual changes in national currency exchange rates
qs.e: Political culture—the shared beliefs, values, and attitudes regarding government—is transmitted and reshaped continuously through political socialization across generations.

qs.q: Communitarian political philosophy challenges Western Liberal Individualism by asserting that individual rights must be balanced with
o: Social responsibilities, communal solidarity, and the common good of society
Unrestricted free-market capital accumulation without taxation
Absolute monarchical authority unconstrained by parliament
qs.e: Communitarians argue that liberal individualism overemphasizes personal autonomy at the expense of social cohesion, contending that rights must be balanced with community duties and common welfare.

qs.q: The exercise of Judicial Review serves as an indispensable constitutional check because it enables courts to
o: Prevent executive excesses and nullify unconstitutional parliamentary legislation
Draft executive tax regulations when parliament is in recess
Appoint state governors during contested local elections
qs.e: Judicial review safeguards constitutional governance by allowing courts to invalidate executive acts or legislative laws that breach constitutional bounds.

qs.q: Under fundamental human rights provisions, the principle of Due Process of Law guarantees that
o: An individual cannot be deprived of life, liberty, or property without fair legal proceedings before an impartial tribunal
The government can seize private property arbitrarily during peacetime
Police authorities can detain suspects indefinitely without court arraignment
Executive ministers can override court judgments through administrative memos
